p-frost-rings: Trees in cold regions sometimes record volcanic eruptions as frost rings, bands of damaged cells formed when an unseasonably cold spell strikes during the growing season.

Because a large eruption loads the stratosphere with sulfate aerosols that dim sunlight for a year or two, researchers have long treated a cluster of frost rings in a single year, across distant continents, as the signature of one.
Several well-known eruptions were dated in this way before ice-core sulfate records confirmed them.
Yet the method has a weakness that its users did not at first acknowledge.
Frost rings also form after ordinary spring cold snaps, and in a region where trees grow near their cold limit, a damaging frost may occur in many years of any century.
A cluster on one continent therefore proves little, and even simultaneous clusters on two continents could arise by chance if the trees sampled are numerous enough.

What distinguishes a volcanic frost ring is not its existence but its position: aerosol cooling tends to strike late in the growing season, producing damage in the outer part of the ring, whereas spring frosts damage the inner part.
When researchers restricted attention to late-season damage, several eruptions once credited to frost-ring evidence lost their support, while others gained it.
Frost rings thus remain useful, but as corroboration of an eruption identified in the ice rather than as an independent detector of one.
p-ocean-iron: In large stretches of the open ocean, nitrate and phosphate are abundant yet phytoplankton remain scarce, a puzzle that was resolved when experiments showed that the shortage was of dissolved iron.

Adding small amounts of iron to surface water produced blooms within days, and the finding inspired the proposal that seeding such regions would draw carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere, since blooming algae absorb the gas as they grow.
The proposal assumes, however, that carbon taken up at the surface stays out of the atmosphere.
Much of it does not: grazers eat the bloom and respire a large part of the carbon back into the water within weeks, and only the fraction that sinks into deep water remains isolated for centuries.
Measurements during the experimental blooms showed that this fraction varied widely, and in some cases was too small to detect.
The difference seems to depend on which organisms bloom; heavy-shelled diatoms sink quickly, whereas soft-bodied species are consumed near the surface.
Iron fertilization has thus been shown to raise growth reliably but to lower atmospheric carbon only in some cases, and a bloom alone cannot show which case obtains.
p-microcredit: Early studies of small loans to poor entrepreneurs reported striking successes: borrowers repaid at rates above 95 percent, and many described rising incomes.
Such accounts encouraged the view that credit was the missing ingredient in poverty reduction.
But borrowers who volunteer for loans are unusually motivated, and a program that reports only their outcomes cannot separate the effect of the loan from the effect of the borrower.
When economists later allocated loans by lottery among similar applicants, the results were more modest.
Businesses grew slightly, and some borrowers bought durable goods, but average household income and spending on health and schooling showed no reliable change after several years.
It would be a mistake to conclude that the loans were worthless.
The averages concealed a small group of borrowers who already ran profitable businesses and gained substantially, offset by others whose enterprises failed and left them with debts.
What the lottery studies undermine is not the existence of benefits but the claim that they are broad.
Credit appears to help those with an opportunity to use it, a narrower finding than the original enthusiasm promised and one that argues for targeting rather than for expansion.
p-retranslation: Translators of a classic often justify a new version by saying that earlier ones have grown dated, as though the original stood still while language aged around it.

The retranslation hypothesis, as scholars call it, holds that a first translation tends to domesticate a foreign work, smoothing its strangeness for readers, while later versions grow progressively more faithful to the original's style.
The hypothesis has an appealing logic: once a work is established in the target language, translators can afford to risk difficulty.
Yet surveys of retranslations of nineteenth-century novels show no consistent drift toward fidelity.
Some late translations are more literal than the earliest; others are freer, written to compete with a rival's version or to suit a new market.

This does not refute the hypothesis, whose defenders point out that the pattern holds more often for works translated under conditions of low risk, such as a prestigious author whose reputation guarantees an audience.
But a hypothesis that applies only to cases in which its conditions are met is no longer a general account of how translation changes; it is a description of one tendency that competes with others.
A more modest conclusion is that retranslations reflect the aims of whoever commissions them, and that fidelity is only one such aim.
p-fresco-blue: When conservators analyzed the blue mantle in a fresco of the Virgin, they found that the visible azurite lay over a layer of cheaper pigment.
Art historians first took this as evidence of fraud: patrons paid by the ounce for azurite, and an underlayer would have let the workshop use less of it.
The inference seems natural, but it overlooks what is known about the technique.
A fresco painter works in sections, each finished before the plaster dries, and an azurite layer applied directly to wet plaster tends to turn dull and greenish.
Applying the mineral over a dry underlayer was a documented remedy, described in at least one workshop manual of the period.
The manual does not settle the matter, since it shows only that the practice was known, not that this workshop used it for that reason.

Still, the thickness of the azurite layer points the same way: it is too uniform and too thick to be a thrifty skim, which suggests that the underlayer was meant to protect the color rather than to save money.
The fraud hypothesis is therefore not impossible, but it now needs evidence that the technical explanation cannot supply.
p-open-plan: Companies that remove walls from their offices usually promise more collaboration, and the promise has some basis: workers within earshot of one another do exchange ideas more readily.
But a study that fitted employees with sensors measuring face-to-face contact found that, after a redesign, such contact fell by roughly two-thirds, while email use rose.
The finding looks like a paradox until one considers what people do when they cannot control their exposure to others.
In a closed office, a person decides when to be available; in an open one, availability is constant, and the cost of being overheard or interrupted makes withdrawal the sensible response.
Workers put on headphones, booked meeting rooms for conversations they once had at a desk, and moved discussion online, where it could be conducted privately.
These adaptations are rational individually, yet the result is the opposite of what the redesign was meant to achieve.
It would be too hasty to infer that open plans never help, since the study examined only two firms, both with employees whose work required concentration.
What can be said is that the benefit of proximity cannot be assumed to survive the loss of privacy, because people respond to a layout, not simply to the distance it creates.
p-oral-epic: Scholars who study oral epic have long argued that a bard composes in performance, assembling each telling from stock phrases and scenes rather than recalling a fixed text.
The theory was developed by comparing living singers with the language of the Homeric poems, and it explained why the same epithets recur so often: a formula is a metrical tool, not a decoration.
It also seemed to imply that a written epic was not oral at all, since a text frozen on the page is the opposite of a song recomposed at each performance.
In several traditions, singers were recorded performing the same epic years apart, and the versions agreed closely in length and in order of episodes, even though the wording varied.
Some singers who had learned to write produced dictated texts that were no less formulaic than their sung versions.
Neither observation shows that the Homeric poems were composed orally; both show that formulaic style cannot serve as proof of oral composition, since a literate poet can adopt it.
The style is therefore evidence of a tradition behind the poems, but of nothing as specific as how the poems were made.

paragraphs: Forests, according to a popular account, are held together by a 'wood wide web': fungi that colonize the roots of neighboring trees connect them in a common network, through which large, established trees pass carbon and warning signals to seedlings.

The account rests on experiments in which labeled carbon, supplied to one tree, was later detected in nearby seedlings, and on observations that seedlings growing near mature trees of their own species survive better when fungal connections are left intact.
Taken at face value, these results suggest that forests behave less like arenas of competition than like cooperatives.
The account has been repeated in books and documentaries, which has given it an authority that the underlying studies, taken one at a time, do not obviously carry.
Careful critics have pointed out how little of this has been shown.

Detecting labeled carbon in a seedling does not reveal how it arrived; carbon can pass through soil as dissolved compounds, or be absorbed after fungal tissue decays, without any living connection delivering it.

In the experiments that did block fungal links while allowing other routes, the amounts transferred were often small compared with what a seedling fixes by photosynthesis, and the survival benefit was frequently no larger than what shade or soil moisture could explain.
Moreover, a transfer that occurs is not shown to be useful to the trees: fungi might shuttle carbon between hosts as a by-product of their own nutritional exchanges.
The language of 'sharing' and 'communication' assigns purposes to processes whose consequences, for the trees, have not been measured.
None of this entails that the networks are unimportant.
Fungal connections are plainly widespread, and there is good evidence that they supply seedlings with nutrients and help them establish themselves in poor soil.

What the critics' objections show is that popular claims run ahead of the evidence, which supports conclusions at the level of individual trees and fungi, not at the level of the forest as a cooperating whole.

Whether the whole-forest claim is true remains an open question, and answering it would require measuring the consequences for tree fitness, which are far harder to observe than the movement of a labeled atom.
Historians of early modern Europe use parish registers of baptisms, marriages and burials to estimate how populations grew.
The method seems to offer something rare for the period: a continuous, local record, kept by one kind of official for centuries.

Because baptisms are the most reliably entered of the three kinds of event, a rise in baptisms has often been read as a rise in births and so as evidence of population growth, particularly in decades when burials did not rise as quickly.
The inference conceals a difficulty.
A register records only those events the parish priest was told about and chose to enter, and in many regions the share of births that reached the register changed over time.

Where a church demanded early baptism, as after doctrinal disputes in the sixteenth century, registration became more complete, and a rise in recorded baptisms could follow with no change in the number of births at all.

Conversely, where some dissenting congregations refused infant baptism, or where families traveled to be baptized elsewhere, a fall in baptisms could reflect religion or migration rather than fewer births.
Compounding the problem, burial entries often omitted infants who died unbaptized, so a register's apparent mortality may be too low exactly when baptism was not universal.
A simple count of entries thus mixes two things, the underlying events and the thoroughness with which they were recorded, and the counts alone cannot separate them.

Demographers have responded with a method called family reconstitution, which links the entries for individual families across registers and thereby allows omissions to be detected: a child who appears in a later burial entry but never in a baptism entry, for example, signals a gap.
The method is laborious and applies only to parishes with unusually complete records, which are unlikely to be typical.

For such parishes the estimates are far more secure, yet the historian who generalizes from them to a region is again relying on an assumption, that the well-kept parish resembles the badly kept one in everything but its bookkeeping.

What emerges is not skepticism about registers but a changed view of what a count of entries is evidence of: until the recording process itself has been investigated, the figures describe the registers as reliably as they describe the population.

p-cr-bike-lanes: After a city installed protected bike lanes on Marsh Street, reported bicycle collisions there fell by 30 percent over the following year.
The transportation department concluded that the lanes made cycling on Marsh Street safer.
It noted that the street's layout, speed limits and traffic signals were otherwise unchanged.
Reported bicycle collisions elsewhere in the city were roughly flat over the same period.
p-cr-tutoring: A school district offered free reading tutoring to every student who scored below a fixed cutoff on a fall test.
When the same students were retested in the spring, the tutored group's scores had risen by an average of 11 points.
The district's board concluded that the tutoring program raised reading achievement.
A skeptical parent replied that students who score unusually low on one test often score higher on the next, simply by chance.
p-cr-compressed-week: A consulting firm's Denver office schedules employees on four ten-hour days a week, while its Austin office uses five eight-hour days.
Both offices employ consultants who do similar client work and are paid on the same scale.
In an annual survey, Denver employees reported markedly higher job satisfaction than Austin employees.
The firm's director concludes that moving the Austin office to a four-day schedule would raise satisfaction there.
p-cr-solar-panels: Utility researchers tracked 600 households that installed rooftop solar panels.
Their total electricity consumption, counting the power produced by the panels, was 8 percent lower in the two years after installation than in the two years before.
The researchers concluded that owning panels makes households more conscious of how much power they use, and they recommended subsidies for panels as an energy-conservation measure.
p-cr-bypass: When a highway bypass opened beside the town of Harlow, traffic through the town's center fell by about a third.
Local merchants had predicted that the loss of passing traffic would hurt their business.
Yet in the year after the bypass opened, revenues at restaurants in Harlow's center rose by 10 percent, and the number of restaurants in the center did not change.
p-cr-tuition-dip: Analysts who predict that higher tuition will cut enrollment at public universities point to the fall in enrollment at several of them after recent tuition increases.
But enrollment at public universities typically falls during economic recessions, whatever happens to tuition.
The recent increases coincided with a recession.
The fall in enrollment therefore cannot, by itself, be taken as evidence that the tuition increases caused it.
p-cr-outdoor-seating: Last year a city health office ranked the restaurants in one district by inspection score.
The district contains 200 restaurants in all, each of which was ranked.
Of the 40 restaurants with the highest scores, 34 offered outdoor seating.
An official concluded that outdoor seating promotes good food-handling practices and urged the remaining restaurants in the district to add it.
p-cr-island-seabirds: Biologists surveying a group of islands found that nesting seabird numbers had fallen sharply on every island where rats had been introduced.
On islands where the rats were later eradicated, seabird numbers recovered within a decade, with one exception: on the islands that also held feral cats, no recovery occurred.
Islands that rats had never reached showed no comparable decline in seabirds.

questions.given: n is a positive integer with exactly 3 positive divisors.
questions.qa: The number of positive divisors of n³
questions.explain: A number with exactly 3 divisors is the square of a prime, n = p². Then n³ = p⁶, whose divisors are p⁰ through p⁶, so 7 of them. Multiplying 3 by 3 to get 9 is the tempting slip; 7 < 9, so Quantity B is greater.

questions.given: x is a prime number.
questions.qa: The remainder when x⁴ is divided by 16
questions.explain: Every odd prime leaves remainder 1 when raised to the fourth power and divided by 16 (3⁴ = 81 = 5 × 16 + 1, 5⁴ = 625 = 39 × 16 + 1), so for those x the quantities are equal. The prime 2 is the exception: 2⁴ = 16, remainder 0, so Quantity B is greater. Two different relationships, so it cannot be determined. The tempting answer is C, from testing only 3, 5 and 7.
questions.why: Every odd prime gives 1, so students answer 'equal'; the only even prime, 2, flips it.

questions.stem: How many positive integers less than 200 are divisible by exactly one of the numbers 6 and 10?
questions.explain: There are 33 multiples of 6, 19 multiples of 10 and 6 multiples of 30 (their least common multiple) below 200. Numbers divisible by both are counted in both lists, so exactly one = 33 + 19 − 2 × 6 = 40. The union, 33 + 19 − 6 = 46, includes the numbers divisible by both and is the tempting answer.

questions.stem: How many three-digit positive integers n leave remainder 3 when divided by 4, remainder 5 when divided by 6, and remainder 2 when divided by 7?
questions.explain: Remainder 3 on division by 4 and remainder 5 on division by 6 mean n + 1 is a multiple of both 4 and 6, so n ≡ 11 (mod 12). Among 11, 23, 35, … the first to leave remainder 2 on division by 7 is 23, so n = 23 + 84k, since 84 = lcm(12, 7). The three-digit values are 107, 191, …, 947 (k = 1 to 11): 11 numbers. The tempting 12 counts k = 0, but n = 23 is not three-digit.
questions.why: The first valid number, 23, is not three-digit, so the usual 'smallest solution plus steps' count is one too high.

questions.stem: How many positive divisors of 7200 are perfect squares or perfect cubes?
questions.explain: 7200 = 2⁵ × 3² × 5². A divisor 2ᵃ3ᵇ5ᶜ is a perfect square when a, b, c are all even: 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 choices. It is a perfect cube when a, b, c are all multiples of 3: a is 0 or 3, b and c are 0, so 2 choices (1 and 8). Both at once means a sixth power, and only 1 qualifies (2⁶ does not divide 7200). So 12 + 2 − 1 = 13. The tempting 14 forgets that 1 is counted in both lists.
questions.why: The number 1 is both a square and a cube, so adding 12 + 2 double counts it.

questions.stem: Several positive integers n have the property that n! ends in exactly 6 zeros. What is the sum of all such n?
questions.explain: Trailing zeros of n! equal the number of factors of 5. 24! has 4 (from 5, 10, 15, 20), but 25! has 5 + 1 = 6 because 25 = 5² contributes two. The count stays 6 until the next multiple of 5, 30!. So n = 25 through 29 work, and the sum is 135. The tempting wrong approach says '6 multiples of 5, so n starts at 30', giving 30 + … + 34 = 160, which misses the extra 5 in 25.
questions.why: Trailing zeros stay constant across a run of five consecutive n, so the answer is a sum over several values, not one.

questions.stem: A positive divisor of 720 is chosen at random, each divisor being equally likely. What is the probability that it is a multiple of 6 or a multiple of 10? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explain: 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5 has 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 divisors. Multiples of 6 are 6 times a divisor of 120, which has 16 divisors. Multiples of 10 are 10 times a divisor of 72, which has 12. Multiples of both are multiples of 30, 30 times a divisor of 24, which has 8. So 16 + 12 − 8 = 20 divisors qualify and the probability is 20/30 = 2/3. Adding 16 + 12 = 28 without removing the overlap gives the tempting 14/15.
questions.why: Divisors that are multiples of both 6 and 10 (multiples of 30) are counted twice unless the overlap is removed.

questions.stem: For every integer n, which of the following expressions is divisible by 6? Indicate all such expressions.
options: n³ + 5n
2n³ + 4n
n³ + 11n
questions.explain: n³ + 5n = (n³ − n) + 6n, 2n³ + 4n = 2(n³ − n) + 6n and n³ + 11n = (n³ − n) + 12n, and n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1) is a product of three consecutive integers, so each is divisible by 6. n(n + 1)(2n + 1) is always 6 times a sum of squares. (n + 1)(n + 2) is the tempting wrong choice: it gives 6 and 12 at n = 1 and 2, but 20 at n = 3. (n + 2)(n + 3) gives 20 at n = 2.
questions.why: (n + 1)(n + 2) passes the first two small tests (6 and 12) and fails only at n = 3; plugging n = 1 and 2 is not enough.

questions.given: x and y are positive integers with greatest common divisor 6 and least common multiple 360.
questions.qa: x + y
questions.explain: Write x = 6a and y = 6b with a and b having no common factor, so ab = 60. The coprime pairs are (1, 60), (3, 20), (4, 15), (5, 12), giving x + y = 366, 138, 114 or 102. The pair (6, 10) would give 96, but 6 and 10 share the factor 2 (then x = 36, y = 60 have GCD 12), so it is not allowed. The smallest valid sum is 102, so Quantity A is greater. Skipping the coprime check gives the tempting answer C.
questions.why: The factor pair (6, 10) gives a sum of exactly 96 but is not coprime, so the GCD would be 12, not 6.

questions.given: x is a positive integer and x² has exactly 9 positive divisors.
questions.qa: The number of positive divisors of x
questions.explain: Exactly 9 divisors means x² = p⁸ or x² = p²q² for primes p and q, so x = p⁴ or x = pq. For x = pq, as with x = 6, x has 4 divisors and the quantities are equal. For x = p⁴, as with x = 16, x has 5 divisors and Quantity A is greater. So it cannot be determined. The tempting answer is C, since testing x = 6, 10 or 15 always gives 4 divisors; only x = p⁴ breaks it.
questions.why: Students factor 9 as 3 × 3 only and miss the single-prime case 9 = 8 + 1, which gives x = p⁴.

questions.stem: For every positive integer n, what is the units digit of 13^(4n+2) × 17^(4n+3)?
questions.explain: Only units digits matter: powers of 3 end in 3, 9, 7, 1 repeating, so 3^(4n+2) ends in 9; powers of 7 end in 7, 9, 3, 1, so 7^(4n+3) ends in 3. The product of units digits is 9 × 3 = 27, which ends in 7.

questions.stem: For how many ordered pairs (x, y) of positive integers is 1/x + 1/y = 1/12?
questions.explain: Multiply out: 12y + 12x = xy, so (x − 12)(y − 12) = 144. Both factors must be positive: if both were negative, each would lie between −11 and −1, and their product could not reach 144. So each pair corresponds to a positive divisor of 144. 144 = 2⁴ × 3² has 5 × 3 = 15 divisors, giving 15 ordered pairs. The tempting wrong count is 8, which is the number of unordered pairs (7 pairs with x ≠ y plus x = y = 24); the question asks for ordered pairs.
questions.why: The rearrangement (x − 12)(y − 12) = 144 is a non-obvious step, and the ordered-pair count (including x = y = 24) is easy to miscount.

questions.given: x² > x.
questions.qa: x + 1/x
questions.explain: x² > x holds when x > 1 or x < 0. For x = 2, x + 1/x = 2.5 is greater than 2. For x = −1, x + 1/x = −2 is less than 2. Different outcomes, so it cannot be determined. The tempting answer is A, from assuming x is positive and remembering that x + 1/x is at least 2 for positive x.
questions.why: Most students read x² > x as x > 1 and pick A; negative x also satisfies it and flips the comparison.

questions.explain: Try x = 1/2: A = 4 − 2 = 2, which is greater than B = 1/2. Try x = 9/10: A = 100/81 − 10/9 = 10/81 ≈ 0.12, which is less than B = 0.9. Different outcomes, so it cannot be determined. As x approaches 1, A approaches 0 while B approaches 1.
questions.why: Small x makes A huge, so one test value suggests 'A greater'; the other end of the interval reverses it.

questions.explain: Splitting into cases: x − 2 = 3x + 6 gives x = −4, and x − 2 = −3x − 6 gives x = −1. Both satisfy the equation. Then |x| is 4 or 1, one above and one below 5/2, so it cannot be determined.

questions.stem: If x is a real number satisfying 4^x + 2^(x + 1) = 8, what is the sum of all possible values of x?
questions.explain: Let u = 2^x, so u² + 2u − 8 = 0 and u = 2 or u = −4. Since 2^x is always positive, u = −4 is impossible, leaving 2^x = 2 and x = 1. The sum of the u roots, −2, is a tempting wrong answer, and 2 comes from reading u = 2 as x = 2.
questions.why: One of the two roots of the u-equation is negative and cannot equal 2^x; the sum of the u-roots (−2) is a ready-made wrong answer.

questions.stem: How many integers x satisfy both |2x − 3| < 11 and x² > 4?
questions.explain: |2x − 3| < 11 means −4 < x < 7, so x = −3, −2, …, 6. The condition x² > 4 means |x| > 2, which removes −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2 (note 2² = 4 is not greater than 4). That leaves −3, 3, 4, 5, 6: five integers. The tempting 4 forgets that −3 also satisfies x² > 4.

questions.stem: What is the sum of all real numbers x that satisfy (x − 2)·√(x + 10) = x + 10?
questions.explain: Two cases hide in this equation. If √(x + 10) = 0, then x = −10 and both sides are 0, so x = −10 works. Otherwise divide by √(x + 10) to get x − 2 = √(x + 10); squaring gives x² − 5x − 6 = 0, so x = 6 or x = −1. Check: x = 6 gives 4·4 = 16 = 16, fine; x = −1 gives (−3)·3 = −9 ≠ 9, so it is extraneous. The solutions are −10 and 6, and the sum is −4. The tempting wrong answer is 6, from dividing by the radical and so losing x = −10; adding both quadratic roots gives 5.
questions.why: Two traps in one: dividing by the radical silently drops x = −10, and squaring introduces the extraneous x = −1; students who handle only one still miss the sum −4.

questions.stem: What is the sum of all real numbers x that satisfy √(5x + 4) − √(x − 1) = 3?
questions.explain: Move one radical: √(5x + 4) = 3 + √(x − 1). Squaring gives 5x + 4 = 9 + 6√(x − 1) + x − 1, so 4x − 4 = 6√(x − 1), that is 4(x − 1) = 6√(x − 1). Let s = √(x − 1): 4s² = 6s, so s = 0 or s = 1.5, giving x = 1 or x = 3.25. Both check: √9 − 0 = 3 and √20.25 − √2.25 = 4.5 − 1.5 = 3. The sum is 4.25. Dividing both sides by √(x − 1) loses x = 1 and gives the tempting 3.25.
questions.why: Dividing by √(x − 1) silently drops the root x = 1 (where it is 0), so students who find only x = 3.25 answer 3.25; trial values of x = 1 to 5 also miss the non-integer root.

questions.stem: The real numbers x and y satisfy x + 2y = 8 and x ≤ 2. What is the least possible value of x² + 4y²?
questions.explain: Substitute x = 8 − 2y: x² + 4y² = 8y² − 32y + 64 = 8(y − 2)² + 32. Without the extra condition the minimum would be 32 at y = 2, but x ≤ 2 forces y ≥ 3, where the expression is increasing. So the minimum is at y = 3, x = 2: 4 + 36 = 40. The tempting 32 ignores the restriction.
questions.why: The unconstrained minimum 32 occurs at x = 4, which the condition x ≤ 2 forbids, so the least value is at the boundary.

questions.stem: Every real number x that satisfies |x − 1| > |x + 3| also satisfies which of the following inequalities? Indicate all such inequalities.
options: x² > 1
x² − 2x > 3
questions.explain: Squaring both sides: (x − 1)² > (x + 3)², so −2x + 1 > 6x + 9, giving x < −1. Any x below −1 is below 0, has x² > 1, and satisfies x² − 2x − 3 = (x − 3)(x + 1) > 0. But x = −2 is a solution that fails x < −3 and |x + 2| > 1, and x = −10 fails x > −5.
questions.why: The solution set is x < −1, not x < −3; each wrong option fails only at a specific solution such as −2 or −10.

questions.stem: If x + y = 5 and 1/x + 1/y = 5/3, what is the value of x²/y + y²/x? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explain: 1/x + 1/y = (x + y)/(xy) = 5/3 gives xy = 3. Then x²/y + y²/x = (x³ + y³)/(xy), and x³ + y³ = (x + y)³ − 3xy(x + y) = 125 − 45 = 80. So the value is 80/3. The tempting 125/3 takes x³ + y³ as (x + y)³. Here x and y are irrational, so solving for them individually is no shortcut.
questions.why: x and y are irrational, so the plug-in route fails; one needs x³ + y³ in terms of x + y and xy, without forgetting the 3xy(x + y) term.

questions.given: The price of an item is reduced by p percent, and then the reduced price is increased by q percent, where 0 < p < q and p < 100.
questions.qa: The final price
questions.explain: The final price is the original times (1 − p/100)(1 + q/100). For p = 20 and q = 25 this is 0.8 × 1.25 = 1, so the prices are equal. For p = 10 and q = 20 it is 0.9 × 1.2 = 1.08, so the final price is higher. For p = 40 and q = 50 it is 0.6 × 1.5 = 0.9, so it is lower. Different outcomes, so it cannot be determined. The tempting answer is A, on the idea that the bigger percent increase must win.

questions.given: x liters of a 30% acid solution are mixed with y liters of a 50% acid solution, where x > 0, y > 0, and the 50% solution contributes more acid than the 30% solution does.
questions.qa: The percent acid in the mixture
questions.explain: The 50% solution contributes more acid when 0.5y > 0.3x, that is y > 0.6x. The mixture is above 40% exactly when it has more of the 50% solution by volume, y > x. With x = 10 and y = 8 (more acid from the 50% solution: 4 > 3) the mixture is (3 + 4)/18 ≈ 38.9%, below 40. With x = 10 and y = 20 it is 46.7%, above 40. So it cannot be determined. The tempting answer is A, from confusing 'more acid' with 'more volume'.
questions.why: 'More acid' from the 50% solution does not mean 'more volume'; the weights are volumes, and the condition leaves both cases open.

questions.given: A car travels the first 40 percent of a trip's distance at 40 miles per hour and the rest of the distance at 60 miles per hour.
questions.qa: The car's average speed for the whole trip, in miles per hour
questions.explain: Average speed is total distance over total time. Take a 100-mile trip: 40 miles at 40 mph takes 1 hour and 60 miles at 60 mph takes 1 hour. The total is 100 miles in 2 hours, so the average is exactly 50 mph, and the quantities are equal. The time spent at each speed is the same, so the average is the plain midpoint of 40 and 60. Choosing A (more distance at the faster speed) or B (average speed is always below the midpoint) are the tempting errors.
questions.why: Two opposite instincts pull toward A and B; only by computing the times does one see that they cancel exactly.

questions.stem: A tank is filled by pipe A alone in 6 hours and by pipe B alone in 9 hours. A drain C alone empties a full tank in 18 hours. With the tank empty, A and C are opened at time 0, and B is opened 2 hours later while A and C stay open. How many hours after time 0 is the tank full?
questions.explain: Rates per hour: A = 1/6, B = 1/9, C = −1/18. With A and C open the net rate is 1/9, so in 2 hours 2/9 of the tank fills. With all three open the net rate is 2/9, and the remaining 7/9 takes (7/9) ÷ (2/9) = 3.5 hours. Total: 5.5 hours. The tempting 4.5 assumes all three were open from the start; 6.5 restarts the clock for a whole tank after B opens.
questions.why: The rate changes partway through, so one overall rate cannot be used; the early fill must be counted, not ignored or restarted.

questions.stem: Positive numbers x, y, z satisfy: x is 60 percent of y, and y is 125 percent of z. By what percent is z greater than x?
questions.explain: Take z = 1. Then y = 1.25 and x = 0.6 × 1.25 = 0.75. The amount z exceeds x is 0.25, and the base is x, so the percent is 0.25 ÷ 0.75 = 33⅓%. The tempting 25% takes z as the base, which is how much less x is than z. The 133⅓% is z as a percent of x, not how much greater.
questions.why: The percent increase is measured against the smaller number x, not z; using z as the base gives 25%.

questions.stem: A 20-liter tank is full of pure juice. Four liters of the contents are removed and replaced by 4 liters of a mixture that is half juice and half water, and the tank is thoroughly mixed. This process is repeated. What is the least number of such replacements after which less than 70 percent of the tank's contents is juice?
questions.explain: Each replacement keeps 4/5 of the juice already in the tank and adds 2 liters (half of the 4 liters poured in), so the juice fraction f becomes 0.8f + 0.1. Its distance from 1/2 shrinks by a factor of 0.8 each time: f = 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.8ⁿ. We need 0.5 × 0.8ⁿ < 0.2, that is 0.8ⁿ < 0.4. Since 0.8⁴ = 0.4096 is just above 0.4 and 0.8⁵ = 0.328 is below, n = 5. After 4 replacements the tank is about 70.5% juice, which is not yet below 70%.
questions.why: The replacement liquid is itself half juice, so the juice fraction approaches 50%, not 0; and after 4 steps the fraction (70.48%) is only just above 70%.

questions.stem: Worker A alone can finish a job in 12 days, and worker B alone in 20 days. They work on alternate days, each working at a constant rate: B on days 1, 3, 5, …, and A on days 2, 4, 6, …. How many days after the start is the job complete? Give your answer to the nearest tenth of a day, counting the final day as a fraction of a day.
questions.explain: In a two-day cycle B does 1/20 = 3/60 and A does 1/12 = 5/60, so 8/60 per cycle. After 7 cycles (14 days) 56/60 is done. Day 15 belongs to B and adds 3/60, making 59/60. Day 16 belongs to A, who needs only 1/60 at 5/60 per day, which is 0.2 of a day. Total: 15.2 days. The tempting 15 comes from 7.5 cycles; 14.8 comes from giving the faster worker day 15.
questions.why: The slower worker starts, so day 15 is B's and leaves a sliver for A on day 16; the order matters.

questions.stem: x, y and z are positive numbers. x is 20% greater than y, and y is 25% less than z. Which of the following statements must be true? Indicate all such statements.
options: x is 10% less than z
x is 5% less than z
z is 10% greater than x
x − y is 1/6 of x
z − y is 25% of z
y is 20% less than x
questions.explain: Take z = 1. Then y = 0.75 and x = 1.2 × 0.75 = 0.9, so x is 10% less than z (true). 'x is 5% less than z' adds the percents instead of compounding them (false). z/x = 1/0.9 ≈ 1.11, so z is 11.1%, not 10%, greater than x (false). x − y = 0.15 is 1/6 of 0.9 (true). z − y = 0.25 is 25% of z (true). y/x = 0.75/0.9 = 5/6, so y is 16⅔%, not 20%, less than x (false).
questions.why: Each wrong statement swaps the base of a percent or adds percents instead of compounding them.

questions.stem: A bag contains only red and green marbles in the ratio 3 to 2. Then 25% of the red marbles and some of the green marbles are removed, and red marbles make up 2/3 of the marbles that remain. What fraction of the green marbles were removed? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explain: Use 3k red and 2k green. Red left: 0.75 × 3k = 2.25k. Red is 2/3 of what remains, so green left is half the red left: 1.125k. Green removed: 2k − 1.125k = 0.875k, which is 0.875/2 = 7/16 of the green marbles. The tempting 9/16 is the fraction of green that was kept.
questions.why: The question asks for the fraction removed, but the natural working finds the fraction kept (9/16).

questions.given: Seven people stand in a row.
questions.qa: The number of arrangements in which Ann and Ben stand next to each other
questions.qb: The number of arrangements in which Ann and Ben do not stand next to each other
questions.explain: Treat Ann and Ben as one block: 6! × 2 = 1,440 arrangements with them adjacent. The total is 7! = 5,040, so 3,600 arrangements have them apart. Quantity B is greater.

questions.given: A deck has 10 cards: 6 red and 4 blue. Two cards are drawn one after the other without replacement, and the first card is not looked at.
questions.qa: The probability that the second card drawn is red
questions.explain: By symmetry the second card is as likely to be any card in the deck as the first, so the probability it is red is 6/10 = 3/5. Directly: 6/10 × 5/9 + 4/10 × 6/9 = 30/90 + 24/90 = 54/90 = 3/5. The tempting answer is D, 'it depends on what the first card was', but the first card is unknown, so we average over both cases.
questions.why: Students think the second draw is affected by the first and answer 'cannot be determined'; with the first card unseen, the probability is unchanged.

questions.qa: The number of ordered triples (a, b, c) of positive integers with a + b + c = 10
questions.qb: The number of ordered triples (a, b, c) of nonnegative integers with a + b + c = 7
questions.explain: Subtract 1 from each of a, b and c: every triple of positive integers with sum 10 becomes a triple of nonnegative integers with sum 7, and adding 1 back undoes it. So the two lists match up one to one and have the same size, without any counting. The tempting answer is B, on the idea that allowing zeros gives more triples; but the smaller sum 7 cancels that exactly.
questions.why: The two conditions look different (10 vs 7, positive vs nonnegative), but a shift of 1 per variable makes them identical.

questions.given: For two events E and F, P(E) = 3/5 and P(F) = 7/10.
questions.qa: P(E and F)
questions.explain: Since P(E or F) cannot exceed 1, P(E and F) = P(E) + P(F) − P(E or F) ≥ 3/5 + 7/10 − 1 = 3/10. The smallest value, 3/10, occurs when E or F always happens, and then the quantities are equal. If the events are independent, P(E and F) = 21/50 > 3/10, so Quantity A is greater. Since the problem does not say which, it cannot be determined. The tempting answer is A, from assuming independence.
questions.why: Nothing says the events are independent: students multiply to 21/50 and pick A, but the minimum possible value, 3/10, equals Quantity B.

questions.stem: How many four-digit positive integers have digits that strictly increase or strictly decrease from left to right (for example, 1357 or 9631)?
questions.explain: Any 4 different digits can be written in only one increasing order and only one decreasing order. Increasing: 0 cannot appear (it would be first), so choose 4 of the digits 1 to 9: C(9, 4) = 126. Decreasing: 0 can appear, as the last digit (for example 3210), so choose 4 of the 10 digits: C(10, 4) = 210. No number is both, so the total is 126 + 210 = 336. The tempting 252 is 2 × 126, and 420 is 2 × 210.
questions.why: The digit 0 is impossible in an increasing number but allowed (last) in a decreasing one, so the two counts differ.

questions.stem: How many distinct arrangements of the letters in the word BALLOON have no two L's next to each other and no two O's next to each other?
questions.explain: BALLOON has 7 letters with L twice and O twice, so 7!/(2! × 2!) = 1,260 arrangements in all. With the L's glued: 6!/2! = 360. With the O's glued: also 360. With both pairs glued: 5! = 120. By inclusion-exclusion, 1,260 − 360 − 360 + 120 = 660. The tempting 540 forgets to add back the 120 arrangements that were subtracted twice.
questions.why: The arrangements with both pairs glued are removed twice, so they must be added back once; forgetting gives 540.

questions.stem: A committee of 4 is chosen from 5 mathematicians and 4 physicists. It must include at least one mathematician and at least one physicist. Two particular mathematicians refuse to serve together. How many committees are possible?
questions.explain: Committees with at least one of each: C(9, 4) − C(5, 4) − C(4, 4) = 126 − 5 − 1 = 120. Remove those containing both feuding mathematicians: the other 2 members come from the remaining 3 mathematicians and 4 physicists with at least one physicist, which is C(7, 2) − C(3, 2) = 21 − 3 = 18. So 120 − 18 = 102. Subtracting all C(7, 2) = 21 pairs gives 99, but 3 of those have no physicist and were already excluded.
questions.why: The 'both feuding' committees that have no physicist were already removed; subtracting them again produces the trap answer 99.

questions.stem: Six people are to be seated at a round table. Two seatings are considered the same if one can be obtained from the other by rotating everyone. Ann and Ben refuse to sit next to each other, and Cal and Dee insist on sitting next to each other. How many different seatings are possible?
questions.explain: With Cal and Dee glued as one unit, there are 5 units around the table: (5 − 1)! × 2 = 48 seatings. Of these, the ones with Ann and Ben also adjacent: 4 units, (4 − 1)! × 2 × 2 = 24. So 48 − 24 = 24. The tempting 48 ignores the Ann-Ben restriction, and 72 (the count with only Ann and Ben apart) ignores the Cal-Dee requirement.
questions.why: Two conditions of opposite kinds (together and apart) must be combined, and each count uses the circular (n − 1)! rule.

questions.stem: How many positive integers less than 1000 have digits that sum to 12?
questions.explain: Treat each number as a three-digit string abc, allowing leading zeros, with a + b + c = 12 and each digit 0 to 9. Without the cap there are C(14, 2) = 91 solutions. A digit of 10 or more breaks the cap: set one digit to at least 10 and distribute the remaining 2: C(4, 2) = 6 ways, for each of 3 digits, 18 in total, and no two digits can both be 10+. 91 − 18 = 73.
questions.why: Stars and bars ignores the digit limit of 9; inclusion-exclusion is needed to remove the over-cap cases.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled three times. What is the probability that each result is at least as large as the one before it (for example 2, 2, 5 or 3, 3, 3)? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explain: Count the outcomes by how many different values appear. All different: each set of 3 values has one increasing order, so C(6, 3) = 20. Exactly two different: choose the repeated value and the other value, 6 × 5 = 30, and each can be written in only one non-decreasing order (for example 2, 2, 5). All equal: 6. Total 56 out of 6³ = 216, so 56/216 = 7/27. The tempting 5/54 counts only strictly increasing results; 1/6 assumes one sixth of outcomes (1/3!) are in order, which ignores repeats.
questions.why: Repeated values are allowed, so the strictly-increasing count 20 is too small; the repeated-value cases must be added.

questions.stem: A bag contains 4 red, 3 blue and 2 green marbles. Four marbles are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that the four marbles are exactly two different colors? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explain: Total draws: C(9, 4) = 126. Subtract the draws using all three colors: (2 red, 1 blue, 1 green) 6 × 3 × 2 = 36, (1, 2, 1) 4 × 3 × 2 = 24, (1, 1, 2) 4 × 3 × 1 = 12, which is 72. Subtract the one-color draws: only all four red works (C(4, 4) = 1), since there are just 3 blue and 2 green. That leaves 126 − 72 − 1 = 53, so the probability is 53/126. Forgetting the one-color draw gives the tempting 54/126 = 3/7.
questions.why: Both the three-color splits (2,1,1) and the single all-red draw must be removed; missing the lone one-color draw gives 54/126.

questions.stem: Here C(n, k) is the number of ways to choose k items from n, and P(n, k) is the number of ways to choose and arrange k items from n in order. Which of the following equal 56? Indicate all such values.
options: The number of distinct arrangements of the letters AAABBBBB
The number of 3-element subsets of {1, 2, …, 9} that contain 9
questions.explain: C(8, 3) = 56, C(7, 2) + C(7, 3) = 21 + 35 = 56 (Pascal's rule), P(8, 2) = 8 × 7 = 56, and arranging AAABBBBB means choosing 3 of the 8 positions for the A's: C(8, 3) = 56. Three-element subsets containing 9 need 2 more elements from the other 8 numbers: C(8, 2) = 28. The tempting 8!/(3! × 4!) = 280 divides by 4! although the word has five B's (3 + 4 ≠ 8); the correct division is 8!/(3! × 5!) = 56.

questions.given: A triangle has sides of length 7, 10, and x, where x is an integer.
questions.qa: The perimeter of the triangle
questions.explain: The integer x must satisfy 3 < x < 17, so the perimeter 17 + x is at most 17 + 16 = 33. It equals 33 when x = 16 (sides 7, 10, 16 do form a triangle) and is smaller for every other x, such as x = 5. So the perimeter can equal 33 or fall below it, and the comparison cannot be determined. Stopping at 'the perimeter is less than 34' and choosing Quantity B ignores that 33 itself is reachable.

questions.skill: Cylinder volume from a rolled sheet
questions.stem: A rectangular sheet of paper measures 20 cm by 12 cm. It is rolled, with no overlap, into a cylinder in two different ways: once so that the 20-cm side becomes the circumference of the base, and once so that the 12-cm side does. What is the ratio of the larger volume to the smaller volume?
questions.explain: Rolling a sheet so that the side of length c becomes the circumference gives 2πr = c, so the volume is πr²h = c²h/(4π). Using the 20-cm side as circumference gives 20² × 12 = 4800 (over 4π); using the 12-cm side gives 12² × 20 = 2880. The ratio is 4800/2880 = 5/3. The tempting 25/9 squares the ratio of the sides, but the height changes too, so only one factor of 20/12 survives.
questions.why: The circumference is squared but the height is not, and the two changes partly cancel.

questions.given: A right triangle has legs of length a and b and a hypotenuse of length 10.
questions.qa: a + b
questions.explain: The 6-8-10 triangle gives a + b = 14, so equality is possible. But the isosceles right triangle has a = b = 5√2, so a + b = 10√2, which is about 14.14 and greater than 14. A lopsided triangle with a = 1 gives a + b of about 10.95, which is less than 14. The relationship changes, so it cannot be determined.
questions.why: The familiar 6-8-10 case suggests equality, but the sum a + b ranges from just above 10 up to 10√2.

questions.stem: Two circles with radii 4 and 9 are externally tangent. A line touches the smaller circle at P and the larger circle at Q and does not pass between the circles (a common external tangent). What is the area of the quadrilateral whose vertices are the two centers, P, and Q?
questions.explain: The radii to P and Q are both perpendicular to the tangent line, so the quadrilateral is a right trapezoid with parallel sides 4 and 9 and height PQ. The centers are 4 + 9 = 13 apart; a perpendicular from the smaller center to the larger radius makes a right triangle with hypotenuse 13 and leg 9 − 4 = 5, so PQ = 12. Area = (4 + 9)/2 × 12 = 78. The tempting 84.5 uses 13, the distance between centers, as the height.
questions.why: The height is the tangent length, found from the difference of radii (5), not the sum; using 13 as the height gives 84.5.

questions.stem: A regular decagon (10 sides) has side length 8. One circle is inscribed in the decagon, touching all ten sides, and another circle passes through all ten vertices. What is the area of the region between the two circles?
options: 8π
questions.explain: Each side is a chord of the outer circle that touches the inner circle at its midpoint. The right triangle formed by the center, that midpoint and one endpoint has hypotenuse R (outer radius), legs r (inner radius) and 4 (half the side), so R² − r² = 16 and the ring has area 16π, whatever the number of sides. Trying to find R and r separately is a dead end without trigonometry, and is not needed.
questions.why: The ring's area depends only on half the side length; with 10 sides the radii cannot be found by hand, so only the R² − r² insight works.

questions.skill: Triangle with given area, two cases
questions.given: In triangle PQR, PQ = 8, PR = 15, and the area of the triangle is 48.
questions.qa: QR
questions.explain: The altitude from Q to line PR has length 2 × 48 / 15 = 6.4, and its foot is √(8² − 6.4²) = 4.8 from P. The foot can lie on the same side of P as R, giving QR² = 6.4² + (15 − 4.8)² = 145 and QR ≈ 12.0, or on the other side, giving QR² = 6.4² + (15 + 4.8)² = 433 and QR ≈ 20.8. One is below 17 and the other above, so it cannot be determined. The tempting choice is 'equal' because 8-15-17 is a right triangle, but that triangle has area 60, not 48, so the angle at P is not 90°.
questions.why: The angle at P may be acute or obtuse, which gives two different triangles with the same area and two sides.

questions.skill: Obtuse triangles and the triangle inequality
questions.stem: A triangle has sides of lengths 7, 24, and x, where x is an integer. For which of the following values of x is the triangle obtuse? Indicate all such values.
questions.explain: For sides 7, 24 and x to form a triangle, 17 < x < 31, so 17 itself fails (it gives a flat, degenerate triangle). If x is the longest side, the triangle is obtuse when x² > 7² + 24² = 625, that is x > 25, so 27 and 30 qualify. If 24 is the longest side, it is obtuse when 7² + x² < 24², that is x² < 527, so x < 23, and 20 qualifies. 23 gives an acute triangle (49 + 529 = 578 > 576) and 25 gives a right triangle.
questions.why: Two separate ranges of x give an obtuse triangle (the obtuse angle may be opposite 24 or opposite x), and 17 is a degenerate trap.

questions.stem: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 9 and BC = 12. Perpendiculars are dropped from A and from C to diagonal BD, meeting BD at P and Q respectively. What is the length of PQ?
questions.explain: Diagonal BD = √(9² + 12²) = 15. In right triangle ABD (right angle at A), the altitude's foot P satisfies AB² = BP × BD, so BP = 81/15 = 5.4. By symmetry the foot Q from C satisfies DQ = 5.4. The feet are therefore 15 − 5.4 − 5.4 = 4.2 apart. The value 5.4 is just BP, and answering with it ignores the second perpendicular.
questions.why: Two perpendiculars are needed; the leg-squared relation gives each foot's distance from an end, and the answer is what is left in the middle.

questions.stem: Square PQRS has vertices in order P, Q, R, S. Point M is the midpoint of side PQ and point N is the midpoint of side QR. Segments SM and PN cross at point X. What fraction of the area of the square is the area of triangle PXM? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explain: Place P = (0, 0), Q = (2, 0), R = (2, 2), S = (0, 2), so M = (1, 0) and N = (2, 1). Line SM is y = 2 − 2x and line PN is y = x/2; they meet at X = (0.8, 0.4). Triangle PXM has base PM = 1 and height 0.4, so its area is 0.2, while the square has area 4. The fraction is 0.2/4 = 1/20.
questions.why: Everything hinges on locating X exactly; eyeballed fractions such as 1/16 or 1/10 are tempting.

questions.given: The graph of y = x² − 6x + k crosses the x-axis at two distinct points, both with positive x-coordinates.
questions.qa: k
questions.explain: Two distinct crossings need a positive discriminant: 36 − 4k > 0, so k < 9. The two roots add to 6 and multiply to k; two roots with a positive sum have a positive product only if both are positive, so k > 0. Hence 0 < k < 9 and k is greater than 0. Using only k < 9 would make the comparison look undetermined, the tempting wrong choice.

questions.stem: Line k crosses the x-axis at (6, 0) and the y-axis at (0, −4). Line m is perpendicular to line k and passes through the point where line k crosses the y-axis. At what x-coordinate does line m cross the x-axis?
questions.explain: Line k passes through (6, 0) and (0, −4), so its slope is 4/6 = 2/3. A perpendicular line has slope −3/2, and line m passes through (0, −4): y = −(3/2)x − 4. Setting y = 0 gives x = −8/3. The value 8/3 comes from using the slope 3/2 with the wrong sign.

questions.given: A line in the xy-plane passes through the point (4, 3) and has a positive x-intercept and a positive y-intercept. The line and the two axes enclose a triangle.
questions.qa: The area of the triangle
questions.explain: If (4, 3) is the midpoint of the segment between the intercepts, the intercepts are 8 and 6 and the triangle has area 24, equal to Quantity B. Another line through (4, 3), with intercepts 12 and 4.5 (check: 4/12 + 3/4.5 = 1), encloses area 27, which is greater. Since both outcomes occur, it cannot be determined. The tempting choice is Quantity A: every line you try at random gives more than 24, because equality happens only for the single line whose midpoint is (4, 3).
questions.why: The area has a minimum of exactly 24 and is larger elsewhere; seeing only the minimum case suggests equality.

questions.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = 4x − x². For how many real numbers x does f(f(x)) = 0?
questions.explain: f(f(x)) = 0 means f(x) = 0 or f(x) = 4 (since 4y − y² = 0 gives y = 0 or y = 4). f(x) = 0 gives x = 0 and x = 4. f(x) = 4 gives x² − 4x + 4 = 0, so only x = 2, because 4 is the maximum value of f (its vertex is at x = 2). That is 3 solutions. The tempting 4 assumes two x-values for each of the two outputs.
questions.why: The output 4 is the maximum of f, so f(x) = 4 has a single (double) root; counting two roots for each output gives 4.

questions.stem: In the xy-plane, a circle has center (3, −3) and passes through the point (6, 1). The circle meets the x-axis at two points and the y-axis at two points. What is the area of the quadrilateral whose vertices are these four points?
questions.explain: The radius is √(3² + 4²) = 5. On the x-axis, (x − 3)² + 9 = 25 gives x = −1 or 7; on the y-axis, 9 + (y + 3)² = 25 gives y = 1 or −7. The four points (−1, 0), (7, 0), (0, 1), (0, −7) are the ends of two perpendicular chords, each of length 8, which are the quadrilateral's diagonals, so its area is ½ × 8 × 8 = 32. Using the diameter 10 for both diagonals gives the tempting 50, but neither chord passes through the center.
questions.why: The diagonals are perpendicular chords of length 8, not diameters; using the diameter 10 twice gives 50.

questions.stem: A function h is defined for all real numbers and satisfies h(x + 4) = h(x) and h(x + 6) = h(x) for every x. It is also known that h(1) = 3 and h(2) = 7. Which of the following must be true? Indicate all such statements.
questions.explain: Since h(x + 6) = h((x + 2) + 4) = h(x + 2) by the first rule and h(x + 6) = h(x) by the second, h(x + 2) = h(x): h actually has period 2. So h(7) = h(1) = 3, h(4) = h(2) = 7 and h(−3) = h(1) = 3 are forced, and h(2.5) = h(0.5) because the inputs differ by 2. But h(6) = h(2) = 7, not 3, and h(0.5) is not tied to h(1) or h(2) by any shift of 2. Working with period 4 alone makes h(7) and h(−3) look unforced.
questions.why: The two periods combine into period 2; with period 4 alone, h(7) and h(−3) look undetermined, and h(6) looks like 3.

questions.skill: Distance from a point to a line
questions.given: Point P lies on the line y = 2x + 3.
questions.qa: The distance from P to the origin
questions.explain: The squared distance from (x, 2x + 3) to the origin is x² + (2x + 3)² = 5x² + 12x + 9. At x = 0 it is 9, so the distance 3 is greater than 7/5; but at x = −6/5 it is 1.8, so the distance √1.8 ≈ 1.34 is less than 1.4. Both cases occur, so it cannot be determined. Both intercepts, (0, 3) and (−1.5, 0), are farther than 7/5, which suggests Quantity A, but the closest point on the line is neither intercept.
questions.why: Both intercepts are farther than 7/5, but the closest point on the line (−1.2, 0.6), which is not an intercept, is nearer.

questions.stem: In the xy-plane, the graph of y = |x − 3| − 2 and the horizontal line y = 2 enclose a triangular region. What fraction of the area of this region lies in the first quadrant (x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0)? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explain: The vertex is (3, −2) and the line y = 2 meets the graph at x = −1 and x = 7, so the triangle has base 8, height 4 and area 16. The part below the x-axis is a similar triangle with height 2 and base 4: area 4. The part left of the y-axis is the small triangle with vertices (−1, 2), (0, 2), (0, 1): area 0.5. The first-quadrant part is 16 − 4 − 0.5 = 11.5, which is 23/32 of the area. Making only one of the two cuts gives the tempting 3/4 or 31/32.
questions.why: Two separate pieces are cut off (below the x-axis and left of the y-axis); making only one cut gives 3/4 or 31/32.

questions.given: A list of seven distinct positive integers has a mean of 10 and a median of 8.
questions.qa: The least possible value of the largest integer in the list
questions.explain: The seven integers total 70 and the fourth is 8. To keep the largest small, make the three below 8 as big as possible: 5, 6, 7, leaving 70 − 26 = 44 for three distinct integers above 8. Since 44/3 ≈ 14.7, a largest value of 15 is tempting, but distinct integers with largest 15 total at most 13 + 14 + 15 = 42. With 16 it works (13, 15, 16), so the least possible largest value is 16: equal.
questions.why: Averaging 44 over the top three suggests 15, but the values must be distinct, which forces the largest to 16.

questions.stem: Five numbers have an average of 18. When one of them, n, is removed, the average of the remaining four numbers is 16. When a different one of them, m, is removed instead, the average of the remaining four is 19. If n is replaced by 2n and m is then removed, what is the average of the four numbers that remain?
questions.explain: The five numbers total 90. Removing n leaves 4 × 16 = 64, so n = 26; removing m leaves 4 × 19 = 76, so m = 14. Replacing n by 2n adds 26, giving 116, and removing m gives 116 − 14 = 102 for four numbers: 25.5. The tempting 20.4 divides 102 by 5, forgetting that m is gone.

questions.skill: Standard deviation after adding a value
questions.given: List X has 10 numbers, with mean 50 and a standard deviation of 4. List Y is formed by adding the two numbers 46 and 54 to list X, so it has 12 numbers.
questions.qa: The standard deviation of list Y
questions.qb: The standard deviation of list X
questions.explain: The mean stays 50, and each new number is exactly one standard deviation (4) from it, so each adds 4² = 16 to the sum of squared deviations. Using the population formula, the sum goes from 10 × 16 = 160 to 192 over 12 numbers: variance 16, SD 4. Using the sample formula, 9 × 16 = 144 becomes 176 over 11: again 16. So the SD is unchanged. Adding spread-out values suggests Quantity A, and adding more numbers suggests Quantity B, but here the two effects cancel exactly.
questions.why: Values exactly one SD from the mean leave the SD unchanged; the 'spread raises it' and 'more numbers lowers it' instincts both mislead.

questions.stem: A list of seven positive integers has a median of 6, a mean of 7, and a unique mode of 8. What is the greatest possible range of the list?
questions.explain: The median is the fourth value, 6, so three values lie at or below 6 and three at or above. The mode 8 must appear at least twice, and only the top three positions can hold 8s; to leave room for a large maximum use 8, 8 in the fifth and sixth positions. Since 8 appears exactly twice, no other value may repeat, so the three smallest values are distinct: at best 1, 2, 3. Then the largest is 49 − (1 + 2 + 3 + 6 + 8 + 8) = 21, and the range is 21 − 1 = 20. Taking 1, 1, 1 would give a larger maximum but makes 1 the mode.
questions.why: The mode must be unique, so the small values cannot repeat; using 1, 1, 1 gives 23 and is wrong.

questions.skill: Effect of adding a value to a data set
questions.stem: A data set of nine numbers has mean 40, median 38, and a positive standard deviation. The number 40 is added to the data set. Which of the following must be true of the new ten-number data set? Indicate all such statements.
options: The mean is 40.
The median is 38.
The standard deviation is less than the standard deviation of the original set.
The range is the same as the range of the original set.
The median is greater than 38.
questions.explain: The new value equals the old mean, so the mean stays 40. The mean always lies between the smallest and largest values, so 40 is inside the old range and the range is unchanged. The sum of squared deviations is unchanged while the count rises, so the standard deviation decreases. The median need not change: if the sixth-smallest value of the old set is 38 the new median is still 38, but if it is 40 or more the new median is 39, so neither median statement must be true.
questions.why: The range survives only because the mean cannot lie outside the data, and the median can go either way.

questions.given: The average score of the students in class X is 70 and the average score of the students in class Y is 80. The average score of all students in the two classes combined is 74.
questions.qa: The number of students in class X
questions.qb: 1.5 times the number of students in class Y
questions.explain: The combined average 74 is 4 above 70 and 6 below 80, so the class sizes are in the inverse ratio of those distances: X : Y = 6 : 4 = 3 : 2, so X has 1.5 times as many students as Y. Equal. Inverting the weights gives X : Y = 2 : 3, the tempting Quantity B.

questions.stem: Each of the following lists contains five numbers between 0 and 10, inclusive. Which list has the greatest standard deviation?
questions.explain: Standard deviation measures distance from the mean, so it is largest when values sit at the two extremes and are split as evenly as possible: three 0s and two 10s (variance 24). One outlier among four 0s gives only 16, pulling values inward (1, 1, 1, 9, 9) gives 15.36, and a middle value cuts it too: 0, 0, 1, 10, 10 gives 22.56 and 0, 0, 5, 10, 10 gives 20. The list 0, 0, 5, 10, 10 looks widely spread, but its middle 5 sits right on the mean and adds nothing to the spread.
questions.why: The middle value in 0, 0, 5, 10, 10 and the near-endpoint 1 in 0, 0, 1, 10, 10 each reduce the spread below the all-endpoint list, though they look almost as extreme.

questions.stem: In a class, the mean test score is 70. The mean score of the girls is 75 and the mean score of the boys is 62. Later, 4 more girls, each scoring 85, join the class, and the class mean rises to 72. How many boys are in the class?
questions.explain: The mean 70 is 5 from the girls' 75 and 8 from the boys' 62, so girls : boys = 8 : 5. Say 8k girls and 5k boys, with total score 70 × 13k = 910k. After 4 girls totalling 340 points join, (910k + 340)/(13k + 4) = 72, so 910k + 340 = 936k + 288, giving k = 2. There are 5k = 10 boys. The tempting 16 is the number of girls.
questions.why: Two stages: inverse-distance weights give the 8 : 5 ratio, then a second mean equation fixes the size; 16 is the girls, not the boys.

questions.skill: Mode, median and range with integers
questions.given: A list of six positive integers has a unique mode of 4, a median of 5, and a range of 6.
questions.qa: The mean of the list
questions.explain: The median 5 means the middle two values sum to 10. For 4 to be a unique mode, the middle values must be 4 and 6 with another 4 below them, so the list starts a, 4, 4, 6, e, f with f = a + 6. If a = 4, the list is 4, 4, 4, 6, e, 10 and its sum is at least 34. If a is less than 4, then 6 can appear only once and e must be at least 7, so e and f are different from 6 and from each other: a = 1 is impossible (f = 7 would force e = 7), and the smallest valid list is 2, 4, 4, 6, 7, 8 with a mean of 31/6, greater than 5. Every valid list has mean above 5.
questions.why: The cannot-be-determined answer looks natural, but the unique-mode and range conditions rule out every list with mean 5 or less.

questions.stem: The mean score of 30 students on a test is 74. The 20 students who passed have a mean score of 80. One of the students who did not pass, who scored 44, retakes the test and passes. What is the mean score of the students who have still not passed?
questions.explain: The 30 students total 2220 and the 20 who passed total 1600, so the 10 who did not pass total 620. Removing the retaker's 44 leaves 576 for 9 students: 64. The tempting 62 (620 ÷ 10) forgets the retaker leaves the group, and 620 ÷ 9 ≈ 68.9 removes the student but not the score.

questions.stem: For a list with an odd number of values, the first quartile Q1 is the median of the values below the list's median, and the third quartile Q3 is the median of the values above it; the list's median itself is excluded from both halves. For a list with an even number of values, each half contains exactly half of the values. The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1. The list 2, 5, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14, 19, 22, 30, 41 has 11 values. If the value 12 is added to the list, by how much does the interquartile range decrease?
questions.explain: For the original 11 values, Q1 is the median of 2, 5, 7, 8, 11, which is 7, and Q3 is the median of 14, 19, 22, 30, 41, which is 22, so the IQR is 15. With 12 added there are 12 values and each half has 6: 2, 5, 7, 8, 11, 12 has median 7.5, and 13, 14, 19, 22, 30, 41 has median 20.5, so the IQR is 13, a decrease of 2. One extra value changes which values form each half and both quartiles move, in opposite directions, so a decrease of 0 or 1 is tempting but wrong.
questions.why: Adding one value changes the parity of the count, so both quartiles must be recomputed with the other rule; they move in opposite directions.

questions.stem: To the nearest whole percent, by what percent did Calder Outdoor's total net sales change from 2024 to 2025?
questions.explain: Convert each line back to 2024 sales: Tents 160/1.25 = 128, Boots 192/1.2 = 160, Packs 128/0.8 = 160, Stoves 96/1.5 = 64, Other 64. The 2024 total is 576, so total growth is 64/576 ≈ 11%. Weighting the changes by 2025 shares gives about 15.75%, and the simple average of the changes gives 15%; both are wrong because each percent change applies to the 2024 base.
questions.why: Weighting the percent changes by the 2025 shares is the natural mistake; the weights must be 2024 sales.

questions.qa: The increase in net sales of Tents from 2024 to 2025, in dollars
questions.qb: The increase in net sales of Boots from 2024 to 2025, in dollars
questions.explain: Tents' 2025 sales are 25% of $640 million = $160 million, so 2024 was 160/1.25 = $128 million, an increase of $32 million. Boots' 2025 sales are $192 million, so 2024 was 192/1.20 = $160 million, also an increase of $32 million. Equal. The tempting error applies 25% and 20% to the 2025 figures (40 versus 38.4), which points to Quantity A.
questions.why: The larger percent change belongs to the smaller base, so the dollar changes coincide.

questions.stem: For which of Calder Outdoor's product lines was the share of total net sales in 2024 greater than the share in 2025? Indicate all such product lines.
questions.explain: Rebuilding 2024 from the 2025 figures gives $128 million (Tents), $160 million (Boots), $160 million (Packs), $64 million (Stoves) and $64 million (Other), a total of $576 million. Total sales therefore grew by 640/576 − 1 ≈ 11.1%. A line loses share exactly when it grew by less than the total: Packs (−20%) and Other (0%). Tents (+25%), Boots (+20%) and Stoves (+50%) all grew faster. Leaving out Other is tempting because its sales did not change, but a flat line is a smaller slice of a bigger total.
questions.why: The benchmark is the total's 11.1% growth: Other (0%) loses share even though it did not fall, and the 2025 shares cannot be compared directly.
options: Tents
Boots
Packs
Stoves
Other

questions.qa: The percent increase in the South warehouse's shipments from January to June
questions.qb: The percent increase in the North warehouse's shipments from January to June
questions.explain: South went from 30 to 60 thousand, a 100% increase; North went from 40 to 70 thousand, a 75% increase. Both rose by 30 thousand, but the same increase on the smaller base (South) is a larger percent. The tempting choice is 'equal', because the absolute increases match.

questions.stem: By what percent would the South warehouse's April-through-June shipments have had to be greater for the combined April-through-June shipments of both warehouses to be 50% greater than the combined January-through-March shipments? Give your answer to the nearest whole percent.
questions.explain: January through March: North 40 + 30 + 50 = 120 and South 30 + 40 + 40 = 110, a total of 230, so the target is 1.5 × 230 = 345. North shipped 40 + 60 + 70 = 170 in April through June, so South would need 175. South actually shipped 50 + 50 + 60 = 160, so it needs 15 more: 15/160 = 9.4%, about 9%. The tempting 5% divides the 15 by the combined 330 instead of South's own total.
questions.why: The percent is relative to South's own 160, not the combined total; dividing by 330 gives 5.

questions.stem: In which of the following months was the North warehouse's share of the combined orders shipped from the two warehouses greater than its share in the month before? Indicate all such months.
options: February
March
April
May
June
questions.explain: North's share is 40/70 = 57.1% in January, 30/70 = 42.9% in February, 50/90 = 55.6% in March, 40/90 = 44.4% in April, 60/110 = 54.5% in May and 70/130 = 53.8% in June. It rose in March and May, when North grew and South stayed flat. In June both warehouses rose by 10 thousand; adding the same amount to both pulls a share above one half back toward one half, so North's share slipped. Choosing June because North's shipments reached their high is the tempting error.
questions.why: North's shipments rise in June, but South's rise by the same amount, so North's share falls (54.5% to 53.8%).

questions.skill: Percent change from a line chart
questions.qa: The percent increase in the museum's attendance from 2021 to 2022
questions.qb: The percent increase in the park's attendance from 2021 to 2022
questions.explain: From 2021 to 2022 the museum went from 100 to 150 thousand, a 50% increase, and the park from 150 to 225 thousand, also 50%. Equal. The park's gain is larger in thousands (75 versus 50), which tempts Quantity B, but percent increase compares gain with each venue's own base.
questions.why: The park's gain is larger in thousands (75 versus 50), which tempts a choice of the park, but the percent increases are the same 50%.

questions.skill: Comparing two series with a threshold
questions.stem: In how many of the seven years shown was the park's attendance strictly greater than twice the museum's attendance?
questions.explain: Twice the museum's attendance versus the park's: 2019 150 vs 150 (tie), 2020 200 vs 175, 2021 200 vs 150, 2022 300 vs 225, 2023 250 vs 250 (tie), 2024 200 vs 225, 2025 250 vs 300. The park is strictly greater only in 2024 and 2025, so the answer is 2. Counting the two exact ties gives the tempting 4.
questions.why: Two years are exact ties at twice the museum's attendance and must be excluded.

questions.stem: Suppose that the museum's attendance falls 20% from 2025 to 2026 and then rises 20% from 2026 to 2027, while the park's attendance rises 10% from 2025 to 2026 and then falls 10% from 2026 to 2027. The museum's 2027 attendance would then be what percent of the park's 2027 attendance, to the nearest whole percent?
questions.explain: Museum: 125 × 0.8 × 1.2 = 125 × 0.96 = 120 thousand. Park: 300 × 1.1 × 0.9 = 300 × 0.99 = 297 thousand. 120/297 ≈ 40.4%, so 40. Treating +20%/−20% and +10%/−10% as cancelling gives 125/300 ≈ 42%, the tempting answer.
questions.why: An up-then-down percent change does not cancel (factors 0.96 and 0.99), and assuming it does gives 42.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: Frost rings cannot be used to date volcanic eruptions, because ordinary frosts also damage trees.
A technique for detecting eruptions relies on a feature that is less diagnostic than assumed, though a more specific feature restores some of its value as corroboration.
Ice-core sulfate records are more reliable than tree-ring evidence, which should therefore be abandoned.
Late-season frost damage is rarer than spring frost damage in trees growing near their cold limit.
Eruptions dated from frost rings before ice-core confirmation were generally dated correctly.
questions.explain: The passage presents a method, shows that its main signal (a frost ring) is common for other reasons, then offers a sharper signal (late-season damage) and concludes that the method is corroborative. The 'cannot be used' and 'should be abandoned' answers are too strong, since the author says frost rings remain useful, and the last answer reports a detail the author later qualifies.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about a year in which trees on two continents show frost damage confined to the inner part of their rings?
options: The year is likelier than most to have followed an eruption, since damage appears on two continents.
No eruption can have occurred, since volcanic cooling damages only the outer part of the ring.
The trees at both sites were growing near their cold limit.
The damage fits ordinary spring cold better than it fits aerosol cooling.
The ice-core record would show a sulfate peak for that year.
questions.explain: Spring frosts damage the inner part of the ring and aerosol cooling tends to damage the outer part, so inner-ring damage is better explained by ordinary spring cold. The tempting answer treats two-continent damage as a sign of an eruption, but the author says such clusters can arise by chance and that position within the ring is what counts. The 'no eruption can have occurred' answer is too absolute, since 'tends to' leaves room for exceptions, and nothing says how close to their cold limit the trees were.
questions.why: The main trap is the two-continent answer: it uses the traditional signature the author has just downgraded, so it sounds like the passage but ignores that position, not location, is the test.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that explains why restricting attention to some frost rings changed which eruptions the method supported.
questions.explain: The sentence beginning 'What distinguishes a volcanic frost ring' explains why: volcanic cooling damages the outer part of the ring and spring frosts the inner part, so looking only at late-season damage separates the two causes. The sentence after it reports that eruptions lost or gained support but does not say why, and the sentence before it only explains why frost rings alone are weak evidence.
questions.why: The following sentence reports the change in which eruptions were supported, so it looks like the answer, but it states the result and not the reason.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following best explains why some experimental blooms removed little carbon from the atmosphere?
options: Grazers consumed the bloom before it could absorb much carbon dioxide.
Too little iron was added to produce a bloom.
The organisms that bloomed were largely soft-bodied and were consumed near the surface.
The blooms lasted only days and so absorbed little carbon dioxide.
The carbon in the bloom was absorbed by deep water before it could be respired.
questions.explain: The passage ties the small sinking fraction to which organisms bloom: soft-bodied species are eaten near the surface, so their carbon returns to the water. The grazer answer is tempting, but grazers eat the bloom after it has absorbed carbon, and the carbon is then respired back, so uptake itself was not the problem. The iron answer contradicts the passage, since blooms did form.
questions.why: The grazer option is a near-miss: grazing is in the passage, but it acts after uptake, not before.

questions.stem: Which of the following would the author regard as relevant evidence for the claim that iron seeding lowers atmospheric carbon dioxide for long periods? Select all that apply.
options: Measurements of the carbon content of particles collected in deep water beneath a bloom.
A measurement of how much carbon dioxide surface water absorbed from the air during the weeks of the bloom.
A record of which kinds of organisms dominated a particular bloom.
questions.explain: The author holds that long-term removal depends on carbon sinking, so measuring carbon in deep water is relevant. The record of which organisms dominated is relevant by inference: the author says the sinking fraction depends on which organisms bloom, and that a bloom alone cannot show which case obtains, so knowing the organisms helps predict whether the carbon stays out. Surface absorption sounds like carbon removal, but the author says much of what is absorbed is respired back within weeks, so it cannot show long-term removal.
questions.why: The surface-absorption measurement sounds like the headline of carbon removal, while the correct organism record is never called evidence in the passage and must be inferred.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the proposal to seed the ocean with iron is best described as
options: guardedly optimistic, since iron has been shown to raise growth reliably
dismissive, because the experiments showed that iron has no effect on growth
cautious, because its premise has been supported but the evidence its conclusion requires is missing
skeptical that iron is what limits growth in these regions
alarmed at the damage that large blooms might do to ocean ecosystems
questions.explain: The author accepts that iron raises growth (the premise) but says a bloom alone cannot show carbon removal (the conclusion), which is caution. The optimistic answer uses the true premise, but the author never shows optimism about the conclusion. The skeptical answer reverses a detail: the passage says experiments showed that iron was what limited growth.
questions.why: The optimistic option is half true (iron does raise growth) and the skeptical one reverses a detail; each fits part of the passage.

questions.stem: The author mentions that borrowers who volunteer for loans are unusually motivated in order to
options: explain why repayment rates in early studies were so high
show that early reports of success could not isolate the effect of the loans themselves
suggest that lotteries select more motivated borrowers than volunteer programs do
argue that motivation matters more than credit in raising incomes
criticize borrowers who exaggerated their incomes to program staff
questions.explain: The motivation point supports the claim that a program reporting only its volunteers' results 'cannot separate the effect of the loan from the effect of the borrower'. The author does not say motivation matters more than credit, only that the two are confounded, and no one is accused of exaggeration.
questions.why: The first option attaches the motivation point to the repayment figure instead of to the confound between loan and borrower, which is its actual job in the argument.

questions.stem: The passage supports which of the following inferences? Select all that apply.
options: In a lottery study, winners' average household income could equal losers' even if some winners gained substantially.
The lottery studies showed that the repayment rates reported in the early studies were overstated.
Loans were more beneficial to borrowers who already ran profitable businesses than to those who did not.
questions.explain: The passage says the averages "concealed" a group that gained substantially, offset by others who were harmed, so equal averages are compatible with large gains for some; and it says the gainers were those already running profitable businesses.
