The repayment option overreaches: the lottery studies challenge what the early success shows about benefits (volunteers were unusually motivated), but the passage never says the reported repayment rates were wrong.
questions.why: The repayment option follows the passage's debunking tone but attributes to it a claim it never makes; the equal-averages option is the hidden case.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?
options: Lottery studies showed that the apparent benefits of small loans were an artifact of borrower motivation.
Randomized evidence shows that early optimism about small loans was overstated, though the loans do benefit some borrowers.
Lotteries should replace voluntary applications as the standard way of allocating loans.
Economists disagree about whether credit can reduce poverty.
Spending on health and schooling is the best measure of a loan's success.
questions.explain: The passage moves from early success reports, to modest lottery results, to the qualification that some borrowers gained. The 'artifact of motivation' answer uses the confound but is too strong, since some borrowers gained substantially, and the author says the studies do not undermine the existence of benefits. The lottery-allocation answer confuses a research method with a recommendation about lending.
questions.why: The artifact-of-motivation option uses the passage's confound but overstates it; the author keeps the benefits for a narrow group.

questions.stem: The author's stance toward the retranslation hypothesis is best described as
options: complete rejection on the strength of surveys of nineteenth-century novels
qualified acceptance: it holds generally once low-risk conditions are specified
recognition that it describes a real tendency, coupled with doubt that it explains retranslation in general
neutral reporting that avoids any evaluation of it
agreement with its defenders that the surveys' counterexamples are irrelevant
questions.explain: The author concedes that the defenders' point means the surveys do not refute the hypothesis, but calls it a description of 'one tendency' and denies that it is a general account. The qualified-acceptance answer sounds balanced but is wrong: the author says a hypothesis restricted to its conditions is no longer a general account, so it cannot 'hold generally'.
questions.why: Two answers sound balanced; only one keeps the author's denial that the hypothesis is a general account.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? Select all that apply.
options: According to the defenders of the hypothesis, a drift toward fidelity should be expected mainly where the risk of failure is low.
Most retranslations of nineteenth-century novels are freer than the first translation.
A retranslation could be less faithful than its predecessor without falling short of the aims of whoever commissioned it.
questions.explain: The defenders say the pattern 'holds more often' under low-risk conditions, and the final sentence says retranslations reflect the aims of their commissioners and that fidelity is 'only one such aim', so a less faithful version can still serve its commissioner's aims. The surveys found no consistent drift in either direction, so no claim that most later versions are freer is supported.
questions.why: The 'freer' option turns the lack of a consistent drift into a different pattern the surveys did not find.

questions.stem: The author refers to 'a prestigious author whose reputation guarantees an audience' in order to
options: give an example of a work whose retranslations, according to the surveys, drifted toward fidelity
give an example of a retranslation written to suit a new market
argue that an author's reputation matters more to a translation's success than its fidelity does
illustrate the kind of case in which, according to the hypothesis's defenders, the predicted pattern is most likely to appear
suggest that the surveys examined works that were unrepresentative
questions.explain: The phrase follows 'conditions of low risk, such as' and so illustrates the low-risk condition under which the defenders say the drift toward fidelity holds more often. The survey answer confuses the defenders' claim with the survey findings, which showed no consistent drift; the 'new market' answer attaches the example to the wrong sentence.
questions.why: The survey option mixes up the defenders' claim with what the surveys found, and the new-market option borrows a detail from a neighboring sentence.

questions.stem: The author's discussion of the workshop manual implies that the manual
options: shows that the technical explanation is more probable than the fraud hypothesis for this fresco
shows that the technical explanation is possible without showing that it is correct for this fresco
contradicts the claim that patrons paid by the ounce for azurite
was written by the workshop that painted the chapel
demonstrates that the fraud hypothesis is impossible
questions.explain: The author says the manual 'shows only that the practice was known, not that this workshop used it for that reason', which is exactly the possible-but-unproven reading. The 'more probable' answer is tempting because it matches the author's own leaning, but that leaning rests on the thickness of the azurite layer, not on the manual. The impossibility answer is the stronger claim the author declines to make.
questions.why: The 'more probable' option is the author's view but not what the manual shows; it rests on the layer thickness.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the fraud hypothesis?
options: Other frescoes by the same workshop show azurite applied over the same cheaper pigment.
A second workshop manual from the period also recommends an underlayer beneath azurite.
Account books show that the patron was billed for much more azurite than the mantle could contain.
Analysis shows that the cheaper pigment was also used elsewhere in the chapel.
The azurite layer varies little in thickness across the whole mantle.
questions.explain: Fraud requires that the patron paid for azurite the workshop did not supply, and billing for far more azurite than the mantle holds is direct evidence of that. Repeated underlayers elsewhere fit both the fraud and the technical explanations, and the second manual and the uniform layer favor the technical explanation.
questions.why: The same-workshop underlayer answer looks incriminating but fits the technical explanation equally well.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which the author concedes a weakness in evidence that the author's own account relies on.
questions.explain: The sentence beginning 'The manual does not settle the matter' concedes that the manual, which the author cites as support, shows only that the practice was known. The final sentence also concedes something ('not impossible'), but it concerns the fraud hypothesis, not evidence the author relies on.
questions.why: The final sentence also makes a concession, so it is a real neighbor trap, but it concedes a possibility, not a weakness in the author's evidence.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: Open-plan offices reduce collaboration and should be abandoned.
Physical proximity does not reliably increase interaction, because people respond to how a layout exposes them.
Email is a more efficient medium for collaboration than conversation at a desk.
Face-to-face contact in offices depends mainly on the physical distance between workers.
A study of two firms shows that workers whose jobs need concentration are unsuited to open plans.
questions.explain: The passage gives a paradox, its explanation (loss of control over availability) and a qualification (only two firms, so no general verdict); the key option captures the explanation and the limit on proximity. The main trap, the 'should be abandoned' answer, is too strong because the author says open plans may still help. The 'physical distance' answer is the very assumption the last sentence rejects.
questions.why: The main trap is the 'should be abandoned' answer, which turns the author's qualified finding into a verdict the author refuses to draw.

questions.stem: The passage supports which of the following about the redesigns it describes? Select all that apply.
options: Some of the communication that disappeared from face-to-face contact continued by other means.
Face-to-face contact fell even though employees were physically closer together.
The redesign reduced the total amount of communication among employees.
questions.explain: Email use rose and discussion moved online, so some communication lost face to face was not lost altogether; and contact fell by about two-thirds even though workers were now within earshot of one another. The total-communication claim is tempting from the two-thirds drop, but it is unsupported: email rose and discussion moved online, and the passage gives no figures showing the overall amount fell.
questions.why: The third option sounds like the obvious takeaway from a two-thirds drop, but the passage gives no total; the first option needs two details put together.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations is most similar in structure to the one the passage describes?
options: A school lets students leave class at any time to ask for help; since leaving visibly marks a student as struggling, students stop leaving, and requests for help fall.
A company installs a suggestion box, but few employees use it because they doubt that management reads the suggestions.
A city widens a highway, and traffic grows until congestion returns to its former level.
A library abolishes late fees, and more books are returned after their due dates.
A company publishes all salaries to build trust; employees who learn they are underpaid grow resentful, and trust falls.
questions.explain: The passage describes a change that makes people more exposed, individuals protecting themselves in a way that makes sense for each of them, and an overall result opposite to the aim. The school case has all three. The salary case has exposure and a reversed result, but the mechanism is resentment, not rational withdrawal. The suggestion box involves doubt, not exposure, and the highway case is a different mechanism (new capacity being filled).
questions.why: The salary option is a near miss with exposure and a reversed result; only the school case has the self-protective withdrawal mechanism.

questions.stem: The author mentions singers who had learned to write and produced dictated texts primarily in order to
options: show that formulaic style also appears in dictated texts, so that written and oral poems can never be told apart
show that formulaic style persists in texts that were written down, which weakens it as proof of oral composition
argue that the Homeric poems were themselves dictated
suggest that written versions of an epic are less formulaic than sung versions
support the claim that stock phrases serve as metrical tools
questions.explain: The dictated texts were 'no less formulaic' than the sung ones, so formulaic style appears in writing too; this is one of the two observations that lead to the conclusion that style cannot prove oral composition. The 'never be told apart' answer overstates this: the author says the style remains evidence of a tradition. The author says nothing about how the Homeric poems were produced.
questions.why: One option overstates the finding into 'never told apart', and another extends it to a claim about the Homeric poems the author leaves open.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the presence of heavily formulaic language in a poem
options: shows that the poem was composed in performance
could have been produced by a poet who composed in writing
shows that the poem was composed by a literate poet
indicates that the poem was sung before it was written down
rules out a long tradition behind the poem
questions.explain: The author concludes that a literate poet can adopt formulaic style, so heavy formulaic language could have been produced by a poet who composed in writing, and it therefore cannot prove oral composition. The 'sung before written' answer is tempting because the style is 'evidence of a tradition behind the poems', but the author says it tells us nothing as specific as how the poems were made.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that gives the reason a formulaic style found in the Homeric poems tells us little about how they were made.
questions.explain: The sentence beginning 'Neither observation shows' gives the reason: a literate poet can adopt the style. The final sentence states what the style does show, which is a conclusion and not a reason.
questions.why: The final sentence also concerns what the style shows about the poems, so it can look like the reason.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Fungal networks among trees probably do not exist.
A widely repeated account of forest cooperation goes beyond the evidence for it, although fungal links are real and probably useful to seedlings.
The popular account of forest cooperation is false, though fungal links help individual seedlings.
Forests are best understood as arenas of competition rather than cooperation.
The functions of fungal networks cannot be studied until tree fitness can be measured.
questions.explain: The first paragraph states the popular account, the second lists what is unproven, and the third says the networks are real and useful while the whole-forest claim stays open. The 'is false' answer sounds balanced but is wrong: the author says the whole-forest claim remains open, not false. The 'do not exist' and 'cannot be studied' answers are stronger than the text.
questions.why: The 'is false' answer sounds balanced but turns an open question into a refutation.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following are reasons for doubting that the labeled-carbon experiments demonstrate cooperation among trees? Select all that apply.
options: Carbon could have reached the seedlings by routes that do not involve a living fungal connection.
Seedlings near mature trees survived no better when fungal connections were left intact.
A transfer of carbon between trees, even if it occurs, has not been shown to benefit the trees.
questions.explain: The critics give two reasons: the carbon might travel through soil or decayed fungal tissue, and a transfer is not shown to be useful to the trees. The 'survived no better' option overstates the passage: it says the survival benefit was often no larger than shade could explain, not that there was none, and the observations described say seedlings survive better with connections intact.
questions.why: The 'survived no better' option distorts 'no larger than shade could explain' into 'no benefit at all'.

questions.stem: The author includes the statement that fungal connections help seedlings establish themselves in poor soil in order to
options: suggest that the critics have misinterpreted the experiments on labeled carbon
provide evidence that forests behave as cooperating wholes
support the claim that fungi deliver warning signals between trees
indicate that the critics' objections concern how far the popular claims go and not whether the networks are valuable
argue that experiments on seedlings are more informative than experiments on mature trees
questions.explain: The statement comes right after 'None of this entails that the networks are unimportant' and gives evidence that some benefit exists, so the critics' objection is to the scope of the claim. The whole-forest conclusion is exactly what the author says remains open.
questions.why: The 'cooperating wholes' answer takes the author's concession for the author's conclusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true of a parish, would most increase a historian's confidence that its recorded baptisms track the number of births?
options: Its register is older than any other in the region.
Burials in the parish rose more slowly than baptisms.
Neither its church's baptism rule nor its families' baptismal practice changed during the period.
Its burial register recorded infants who died before they could be baptized.
It recorded more baptisms in a typical year than any neighboring parish did.
questions.explain: The passage names three ways in which recorded baptisms can drift from births: changing church rules, dissent, and baptism elsewhere. A parish where practice stayed fixed removes the drift, so the count is a steadier index of births. The burial-register option is tempting but concerns burials and mortality, not whether baptisms were recorded. The slower rise in burials is the historians' original reasoning, which the passage says fails to address recording practices.
questions.why: The burials option repeats the very reasoning the passage criticizes.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following could make a fall in recorded baptisms an unreliable sign of fewer births? Select all that apply.
options: Some residents joined a congregation that did not baptize infants.
The church relaxed a rule requiring early baptism.
Burials were entered more thoroughly than baptisms.
questions.explain: The passage says demanding early baptism made registration more complete, so relaxing the demand would make registration less complete and a fall in recorded baptisms could follow with no change in births; and it names dissenting congregations that refused infant baptism as another such cause. Thorough burial entries do not change the baptism count, and the passage says baptisms are the most reliably entered of the three kinds of event.
questions.why: The early-baptism rule is stated only in its tightening form, so students must reverse it; the burial option is register trouble that does not touch the baptism count.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward family reconstitution is best described as
options: dismissive of it, because it applies only to unusual parishes
confident that it settles the problem of omissions for the parishes it covers and so for the region
appreciative of its rigor, but unwilling to treat its results as representative without a further assumption
convinced that the thoroughness of recording can never be measured
indifferent between it and a simple count of entries
questions.explain: The author calls the estimates 'far more secure' but notes that generalizing from well-kept parishes assumes they resemble the badly kept ones. The 'settles it for the region' answer is right about those parishes but wrong about the region, which is the assumption the author flags. The author also does not claim recording can never be measured, only that it must be investigated.
questions.why: The author both praises and limits the method, and the 'settles it for the region' option keeps the praise while dropping the limit.

questions.stem: The biographer's tone is so ______ that a reader might assume the family commissioned the book; even the subject's two bankruptcies are explained away as bad luck.
questions.explain: A tone a family would approve of, in which even bankruptcies are excused, is uncritical praise: adulatory. Elegiac is the tempting choice, since a family-backed book might be mournful, but nothing in the sentence concerns grief. Candid would expose the flaws rather than excuse them, dispassionate describes detachment, and laconic concerns brevity.
questions.why: Elegiac and candid tempt students who think about what a family would want or how an intimate biography sounds, while the real clue is the habit of excusing every failure.

questions.stem: Although the senator's speech was widely praised as ______, its central proposal was a recycled version of a bill that had twice failed.
questions.explain: 'Although' sets the praise against the fact that the proposal was recycled, so the praise must have been for novelty: pioneering. Sonorous is the tempting choice because it describes a speech, but praise for its sound would not clash with a recycled proposal. Doctrinaire, conciliatory and laconic have no link to originality.

questions.stem: Critics accused the economist of being ______ in her use of data: she cited only the studies that supported her thesis and never mentioned the larger body of contrary evidence.
questions.explain: Citing only supportive studies and omitting contrary evidence is slanted advocacy, which is what tendentious means. Fastidious (painstaking) is the opposite of what the critics allege. She is not shy (diffident) or wordy (prolix), and credulous (gullible) misses that her selection of evidence is deliberate.
questions.why: Credulous and fastidious tempt students who read the sentence as being about carelessness rather than slanted, deliberate selection.

questions.stem: By publishing the dissenting opinion in full, rather than allowing it to be ______ in an appendix that few members ever read, the committee signaled a new willingness to let disagreement be seen.
questions.explain: The contrast is between full publication and an appendix few people read, where the opinion would be hidden from view: buried. Condensed and paraphrased are tempting because they echo 'in full', but a shortened or reworded opinion would still be visible, so they do not capture the loss of visibility. Annotated adds commentary and hides nothing, and diluted does not fit a position placed in an appendix.

questions.stem: Critics who call the novel's ending (i)______ overlook how thoroughly the earlier chapters prepare for it; they mistake for (ii)______ twists what has been quietly foreshadowed from the first page.
questions.explain: Foreshadowing shows the ending was prepared, so the critics' complaint must be that it came from nowhere: arbitrary, and the twists they take to be unprepared are unearned. Predictable is the trap in the first blank: a critic who found the ending predictable would be noticing the preparation, not overlooking it. Telegraphed in the second blank describes what the foreshadowing really did, so it cannot be what the critics mistake it for.
questions.why: Predictable and telegraphed both describe a foreshadowed ending accurately, so they tempt students who forget that the critics are the ones who overlook the preparation.

questions.stem: Hailed as a (i)______ of the old orthodoxy, the new study in fact (ii)______ it, supplying numbers where earlier researchers had relied on assumption.
questions.explain: 'Hailed as ... in fact' signals a reversal, and supplying numbers where others had only assumed shows the study supports the orthodoxy: it bolsters it, so the hailing must have been as a refutation. Supersedes is tempting because the study is new and the orthodoxy old, but replacing a view is not what supplying its missing evidence does. Revival and sequel remove the reversal, and qualifies implies adding caveats.

questions.stem: Because the treaty's language was deliberately (i)______, each signatory could claim that it vindicated its own position; that flexibility made agreement possible, but it later made the provisions (ii)______ to enforce.
questions.explain: If every signatory could claim its own position was vindicated, the language allowed several readings: equivocal. Provisions that mean different things to different parties are hard to enforce: arduous. Conciliatory is tempting because the vagueness made agreement possible, but it describes a spirit, not language open to competing readings; inconsequential fits vague provisions but not the sense of 'to enforce'. Categorical would leave no room for competing claims, and facile reverses the cost implied by 'but'.
questions.why: The second blank depends on seeing that the flexibility praised in the first half is the cost named in the second.

questions.stem: The memoirist is (i)______ about her own motives, confessing to petty envy and vanity, yet remarkably (ii)______ toward the colleagues who wronged her, describing them without a trace of rancor.
questions.explain: Confessing to envy and vanity is candid disclosure of motives. Self-effacing is the tempting alternative, but downplaying oneself is not the same as revealing one's motives. 'Yet' and 'without a trace of rancor' call for a generous attitude to the colleagues: charitable. Ingratiating suggests flattery to win favor, which the sentence does not imply, and vindictive is the reverse.

questions.stem: Historians once dismissed the diary as (i)______ because it records little but household chores and weather; yet that very (ii)______ is what now makes it invaluable, since it preserves the texture of ordinary life that official chronicles never noticed.
questions.explain: A diary of chores and weather would be dismissed as inconsequential, and 'that very' feature, its everyday quality, is the mundanity that now gives it value. Insularity is tempting for a household diary, but its value lies in the texture of ordinary life, not in narrowness. Tendentious (slanted) and scandalous describe content the diary is never said to have, and eloquence is not what chores and weather offer.
questions.why: The same feature (the ordinary content) is the reason for both the dismissal and the later value, so the two blanks must describe it consistently.

questions.stem: Although the chief executive publicly (i)______ the merger as a partnership of equals, internal records show that the smaller firm's managers were routinely (ii)______ on key decisions, so the claim of parity was largely rhetorical.
questions.explain: Publicly presenting the merger as a partnership of equals is touting it; lamenting or concealing it would not be a claim of parity. Because the claim of parity was 'largely rhetorical', the managers must have been overruled on key decisions. Consulted is the tempting choice, since it fits the language of partnership, but it would support the claim, not undercut it. Flattered fits grammatically but says nothing about who decided.

questions.stem: A theory that can accommodate any conceivable observation may appear (i)______, but this very (ii)______ is its weakness: because no evidence could count against it, none can count for it either.
questions.explain: A theory that fits any observation looks impregnable, and 'this very' feature, its elasticity, is the weakness explained in the rest of the sentence. Unfalsifiable is the strong trap in the first blank: it names the weakness, but the blank needs an apparent strength. Specificity is the opposite of a theory that fits everything, and novelty is not mentioned.
questions.why: Unfalsifiable is the weakness itself, so it tempts students who skip the 'appear ... but' contrast; the first blank needs the apparent strength, the second a different word for what causes the weakness.

questions.stem: The architect's early work was marked by ornament so (i)______ that the eye found nowhere to rest; after the war, however, she embraced such (ii)______ that critics said her buildings had been stripped to their bare structure.
questions.explain: Ornament so abundant that the eye found nowhere to rest was profuse, and the contrast with buildings later stripped bare points to austerity. Meretricious (showy and cheap) is tempting for ornament critics might dislike, but it describes quality, not the amount that "so ... that the eye found nowhere to rest" requires; cheapness would not by itself leave the eye no rest. Restrained ornament would leave the eye room, and opulence or eclecticism would not strip a building bare.

questions.stem: Scholars long suspected that the manuscript was (i)______, but recent ink analysis, far from (ii)______ that suspicion, has (iii)______ the claim of authenticity by dating the pigments to the very decade the document purports to come from.
questions.explain: A suspicion that bears on authenticity is that the manuscript was spurious (fake). Pigments from the claimed decade support authenticity, so the analysis, far from confirming the suspicion, has vindicated the claim. 'Dispelling' would remove the contrast signaled by 'far from', and undercut or qualified would weaken the claim the evidence supports.
questions.why: The first blank sets up a suspicion of forgery, and 'far from dispelling' is the trap: students who accept it reverse the logic, since evidence supporting authenticity runs against that suspicion, so the second and third blanks must be consistent with each other.

questions.stem: The reformer's rhetoric was (i)______, promising a sweeping transformation of the system, but her actual program proved (ii)______: a handful of procedural changes that left the existing distribution of power (iii)______.
questions.explain: Rhetoric that promises a sweeping transformation is grandiose. 'But' and 'a handful of procedural changes' make the program circumscribed (narrow in scope), and changes of that kind leave the distribution of power undisturbed. Draconian is tempting for a program of procedural changes, but a handful of them is not severe. 'Upended' for the power structure would repeat the promise instead of contrasting with it.
questions.why: Each blank is set by the contrast between promise and result, so a wrong choice in one blank breaks the other two; draconian tempts students who confuse narrow with harsh.

questions.stem: Because the survey's questions were phrased in terms that respondents found (i)______, answers varied widely even when the same respondent was interviewed twice; the researchers, rather than (ii)______ the variation as random noise, treated it as evidence that the underlying concept was (iii)______.
questions.explain: Answers that change even for the same person point to wording respondents could not make sense of: opaque, not transparent, and offensive wording would produce refusals rather than shifting answers. 'Rather than' calls for dismissing the variation as noise; eliminating and concealing do not describe treating something as noise. Contested is the nuance trap in the last blank, since varied answers look like disagreement, but one person giving different answers is not a dispute among people: the unclear wording points to an ill-defined concept.
questions.why: Contested is tempting because varied answers look like disagreement; the same-respondent detail rules out a dispute between people and carries the unclear wording through to the concept itself.

questions.stem: The philosopher's prose is so (i)______ that seminars spend weeks on a single chapter, yet her arguments are so (ii)______ that even her opponents concede she cannot be ignored; later admirers have tended to (iii)______ the difficulty as inseparable from the depth of the work.
questions.explain: Prose that takes seminars weeks to get through is turgid (heavy and difficult); lucid or playful prose would not. 'Yet' and opponents who cannot ignore her call for compelling arguments. Abstruse is the trap: it carries the difficulty of the first blank into the second, but difficulty would not force opponents to engage. Admirers who see the difficulty as inseparable from depth would prize it, not regret or try to simplify it.
questions.why: Abstruse repeats the difficulty from the first blank; 'yet' requires a quality that forces opponents to engage, and the third blank must then be consistent with admirers who accept the difficulty.

questions.stem: Supporters of the policy cite its (i)______ record, noting that none of the pilot programs failed; yet that record is partly (ii)______, since only communities already inclined to succeed volunteered, so the apparent success may be less a (iii)______ of the policy than of the participants.
questions.explain: No failures means an unblemished record. 'Yet' and the fact that only communities already inclined to succeed volunteered make the record partly illusory: it reflects who took part, not the policy's effect. Anomalous is tempting, since a perfect record looks unusual, but an unusual record is not the same as a misleading one. The success is then less a product of the policy than of the participants; prerequisite is tempting but reverses who supplies what. Exemplary would praise the record instead of qualifying it.
questions.why: The trap is self-selection: the record looks strong because volunteers were already likely to succeed, so the second blank must say the record misleads, not merely that it is unusual.

questions.stem: Though the poem has been read as a (i)______ lament for a vanished way of life, its imagery is oddly (ii)______: the farmhouse is described with such clinical detachment that the nostalgia seems to belong to the reader rather than to the speaker, who (iii)______ any sentimental attachment.
questions.explain: A lament for a vanished world is wistful. 'Though' and 'clinical detachment' make the imagery unsentimental; elegiac is tempting because of 'lament', but it would be mournful, not detached. A speaker whose attachment is only the reader's projection disclaims any sentimental feeling. Betrays is a nuance trap (it means to reveal unwittingly), which contradicts the detachment, and avows would contradict it openly.
questions.why: Elegiac and betrays are each tempting for a poem read as a lament, but both clash with the detachment described in the colon clause.

questions.stem: The spokesperson's reply was deliberately ______: after twenty minutes of questions, the reporters left the briefing with exactly the questions they had brought in.
options: candid
noncommittal
pugnacious
equivocal
tactful
diplomatic
questions.explain: A reply built so that nothing can be pinned down is noncommittal and equivocal, and those two give the same meaning. Tactful and diplomatic form a tempting pair, since a spokesperson is expected to be smooth, but they describe the manner of the reply, and a tactful reply can still answer every question; only noncommittal and equivocal explain why the reporters learned nothing. Candid would have answered the reporters, and pugnacious (aggressive) is not suggested.
questions.why: Tactful and diplomatic are a matched pair that tempts students who read the sentence as being about manner; the colon asks for the reply's content, which only noncommittal and equivocal supply.

questions.stem: Although the engineers had hoped to ______ the river's seasonal floods, they could only blunt the worst of them, since the largest surges still overtopped the spillways.
options: eliminate
predict
eradicate
document
mitigate
moderate
questions.explain: 'Could only blunt the worst' shows the original hope was more ambitious: eliminate and eradicate match. Mitigate and moderate form a tempting pair, but they mean about the same as 'blunt', which is what the engineers did achieve, so they would erase the 'although' contrast. Predicting or documenting floods would not be contrasted with blunting them.

questions.stem: The study's conclusions, though stated with great confidence, rest on a ______ foundation: the sample consisted of nine volunteers, all drawn from a single laboratory.
options: parochial
tenuous
novel
flimsy
insular
ornate
questions.explain: Nine volunteers from one laboratory is a thin basis for confident claims: tenuous and flimsy give the same meaning. Parochial and insular are a decoy pair invited by 'a single laboratory', but they describe a narrow outlook, not how weak a foundation is. Novel and ornate say nothing about the strength of the evidence.
questions.why: Parochial and insular are a matching pair that fits the 'single laboratory' detail, so students who match words to the nearest clue choose them instead of the pair about strength.

questions.stem: Rather than ______ a settlement, the mediator let the talks run for weeks, offering her own proposal only once each side had exhausted its grievances.
options: hasten
propose
oppose
expedite
broach
celebrate
questions.explain: Letting the talks run for weeks before proposing anything is the opposite of rushing: hasten and expedite match. Propose and broach are a tempting pair, but the sentence says she did offer a proposal in the end, so 'rather than propose a settlement' would contradict it; the contrast is about speed, not about whether a settlement was raised. Opposing or celebrating a settlement does not fit the contrast.

questions.stem: The author's later novels are often described as ______ versions of her debut, since they rework its plot and cast with only cosmetic changes.
options: radical
derivative
expanded
imitative
parodic
satirical
questions.explain: Novels that rework a debut's plot and cast with only cosmetic changes are derivative and imitative. Parodic and satirical are a tempting pair because 'versions of her debut' suggests commentary on it, but nothing suggests mockery. 'Radical' contradicts the cosmetic changes and 'expanded' implies substantial added material.
questions.why: Parodic and satirical match each other and the idea of a 'version' of another work, but the clue gives no sign of mockery; radical and expanded are wrong because the changes are only cosmetic.

questions.stem: Because the senator's stance on trade shifted with each audience he addressed, observers found it impossible to describe his position as ______.
options: opportunistic
steadfast
mercurial
consistent
cynical
pragmatic
questions.explain: A stance that changes with every audience cannot be called steadfast or consistent. Opportunistic, mercurial, cynical and pragmatic could all describe such a stance, so none is something observers would find impossible to say.
questions.why: The blank names what the stance was not; students who choose words describing the shifting stance (opportunistic, mercurial) reverse the logic.

questions.stem: The critic argued that the film's ______ plot, in which each rescue arrived at precisely the moment the screenwriter needed it, undermined its claim to realism.
options: intricate
contrived
harrowing
artificial
convoluted
byzantine
questions.explain: Rescues timed to suit the screenwriter make a plot feel engineered: contrived and artificial. Convoluted and byzantine are a matching pair tempting for a plot full of well-timed events, but they describe complexity, which nothing in the sentence mentions and which would not undermine realism the way manufacture does. Intricate is likewise about complexity, and harrowing describes the viewer's experience.
questions.why: Intricate, convoluted and byzantine all describe a complicated plot and tempt students who match 'plot' with complexity; the clue is about manufactured timing, not complexity.

questions.stem: The ______ of the old regime's final years, when ministers openly sold offices to the highest bidder, convinced even loyal subjects that reform could no longer be postponed.
options: piety
venality
profligacy
corruption
stability
extravagance
questions.explain: Ministers who sold offices to the highest bidder were corrupt for pay: venality and corruption match. Profligacy and extravagance are a pair that would also push reform, but they mean overspending, not corruption for pay. Piety would be a reason to trust the regime, and stability would not convince loyal subjects that reform was urgent.
questions.why: Profligacy and extravagance form a matching pair that also suggests a regime in decline, but they describe wasteful spending, not selling offices for payment.

questions.stem: Reviewers praised the memoir's ______ prose, noting that she had cut every adjective her editor would allow.
options: florid
austere
ornate
candid
verbose
spartan
questions.explain: A writer who strips out every adjective produces austere, spartan prose. Florid and ornate are a matching pair for the opposite, an ornamented style, and verbose is wordy. Candid is a common word of praise for memoirs, but cutting adjectives says nothing about honesty.

questions.stem: Negotiators over three decades had failed to bridge even the smallest differences, so the treaty that finally resolved them was hailed as ______.
options: unprecedented
overdue
momentous
unparalleled
belated
routine
questions.explain: Three decades in which no negotiator closed even the smallest gap mean that a treaty resolving them had no precedent: unprecedented and unparalleled give the same sentence. Overdue and belated form a tempting pair because of the three decades, but 'hailed as' signals praise, and calling a treaty late is not praise; the sentence's logic is about the achievement having never happened before. Momentous fits alone but has no partner, and routine contradicts the decades of failure.
questions.why: Overdue/belated is the trap pair suggested by 'three decades'; it fails because 'hailed as' calls for praise of the achievement, not a complaint about timing.

questions.stem: The chemist's ______ about the new compound's safety, evident in his insistence on a fourth round of tests, struck the team as excessive but not unreasonable.
options: caution
complacency
wariness
insouciance
certainty
hostility
questions.explain: Insisting on yet another round of tests shows care about a possible risk: caution and wariness match. Complacency and insouciance are a matching pair for the opposite attitude, so they tempt students who read 'excessive' as criticism of carelessness. Certainty would not lead to more testing, and hostility is too strong for something the team found 'not unreasonable'.

questions.stem: The company's earnings, propped up for years by a single patent, proved ______ once competitors introduced cheaper generics: within eighteen months its profits had collapsed.
options: embellished
fragile
negligible
overstated
precarious
lucrative
questions.explain: Earnings that collapsed within eighteen months once the patent lost its protection were fragile and precarious. Embellished and overstated are a matching pair tempted by 'propped up', but the competition exposed weakness; it did not reveal misreporting. The earnings were large enough to collapse, so negligible does not fit, and lucrative ignores the collapse.
questions.why: Embellished and overstated form a matching pair suggested by 'propped up', but the sentence is about how easily the earnings fell, not about their accuracy.

questions.stem: Far from being a ______ observer of the dispute, the consultant had drafted the very proposal that one side was now defending.
options: partisan
disinterested
candid
neutral
zealous
ardent
questions.explain: 'Far from being' means the consultant was the opposite of an impartial observer, since he had written one side's proposal: disinterested and neutral. The trap is disinterested, which students often take to mean uninterested; its real meaning is impartial. Partisan, zealous and ardent describe what he really was, so 'far from' rules them out; candid is not forced by the clue.
questions.why: Disinterested means impartial, not uninterested, and partisan, zealous and ardent describe the consultant accurately, so they are the words most likely to be picked by someone who forgets that 'far from' reverses the sense.

questions.stem: Some commentators dismiss the mayor's policy as ______, since it treats a symptom of the housing shortage without touching its causes.
options: piecemeal
cosmetic
incremental
superficial
punitive
overdue
questions.explain: A policy that deals only with a symptom and ignores the causes is cosmetic and superficial. Piecemeal and incremental are a tempting pair, but they mean done step by step, not leaving the causes alone. Punitive and overdue are not supported by the clue.
questions.why: Piecemeal and incremental match each other and sound like criticism of a limited policy, but they describe the pace, not the failure to address causes.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the department's conclusion?
options: Reported collisions on the parallel streets rose slightly during the same year.
Collisions between cars and pedestrians on Marsh Street did not decline over the year.
Most cyclists surveyed on Marsh Street said they felt safer after the lanes opened.
Bicycle traffic on Marsh Street fell by more than half during the year.
Reported bicycle collisions on Marsh Street had been fairly stable in each of the five years before the lanes opened.
questions.explain: The department counted collisions, not collisions per cyclist. If bicycle traffic on Marsh Street fell by more than half, a 30 percent drop in collisions would mean each remaining rider was less safe, not safer. The rise on parallel streets is the tempting choice, but it says nothing about whether Marsh Street became safer for those who still use it. The car-pedestrian option sounds relevant but concerns a different kind of collision. The surveyed feelings and the stable earlier years strengthen the conclusion.
questions.why: The statistic counts collisions, not collisions per rider, so a drop in riders can explain it; the parallel-street option and the car-pedestrian option sound relevant but do not touch that gap.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the board's conclusion?
options: The students who gained most were those whose fall scores were furthest below the cutoff.
The tutored students' spring scores were still below the district average.
Students who scored just above the cutoff, and so were not tutored, improved by an average of only 2 points between the same two tests.
Among tutored students, those who attended more sessions gained more points on average than those who attended fewer.
A neighboring district reported gains from a similar tutoring program.
questions.explain: The skeptic offers an alternative explanation: low scorers tend to improve by chance. Students just above the cutoff are almost identical in ability but received no tutoring and gained far less, which makes chance a poorer explanation. The tempting option about students furthest below the cutoff sounds like strong evidence, but it is exactly what regression to the mean predicts, so it favors the skeptic. The link between attendance and gains is real but weaker, since more motivated students may attend more. Another district's results are indirect, and the spring scores being below average neither helps nor harms.
questions.why: The skeptic's point is regression to the mean, so only a comparison group answers it; the 'furthest below the cutoff' option sounds like evidence but fits chance.

questions.stem: The director's conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Denver employees rate their schedule as the best feature of their jobs.
All Denver employees prefer their present schedule to a five-day week.
Austin employees are not, on the whole, less suited to a ten-hour day than Denver employees.
Satisfaction with a schedule is the main factor in how long employees stay with the firm.
No office of the firm other than Denver has tried a four-day schedule.
questions.explain: The director reasons from a difference between offices to the effect of changing a schedule, so she must assume Austin's employees would respond to a ten-hour day as Denver's do. If they are less suited to it, for example because of longer commutes, moving Austin to four days would not raise satisfaction. 'Best feature of their jobs' is tempting but not needed, since the schedule could raise satisfaction without being the top-rated feature. 'All Denver employees prefer' is too strong, and retention and other offices' history are not needed.
questions.why: The tempting 'best feature' and 'all prefer' options both sound like support but are not needed; the necessary assumption concerns whether Austin's employees would respond as Denver's do.

questions.stem: Answering which of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the researchers' conclusion?
options: Did the households that installed panels receive a government subsidy toward the cost?
Did panel owners' electricity consumption fall more in the second year than in the first?
Was the 8 percent reduction larger than the savings that other conservation measures typically produce?
Had the households' electricity consumption already been falling in the years before they installed panels?
Do the households that installed panels earn more than the average household?
questions.explain: The conclusion is causal: panels make households use less. If consumption had been falling before the panels went in, the drop may be a continuation of that trend, which would undercut the claim; if it had been flat, the claim gains support. Whether the drop grew in the second year is tempting but fits either story. The subsidy and the comparison with other measures bear on the recommendation, not on whether panels caused the drop, and household income does not decide the question.
questions.why: The key question concerns the pre-installation trend (an alternative cause); the subsidy, second-year and comparison questions bear on the policy or fit either answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy?
options: Traffic on the bypass exceeded the planners' forecasts.
Before the bypass, traffic through the town center was heaviest on weekday mornings.
Revenues at retail shops in Harlow's center, which also depend on passing traffic, fell during the same year.
Most of the traffic diverted to the bypass was trucks bound for other towns, whose congestion had kept many residents from going into the center.
Before the bypass, restaurants in Harlow's center had drawn about a third of their customers from through travelers.
questions.explain: The puzzle is why restaurant revenue rose when traffic fell. If the vanished traffic was mostly through-trucks that had clogged the center and kept residents away, the restaurants lost few customers and gained local diners once the streets cleared, which accounts for the rise. The fall in retail revenue and the restaurants' earlier reliance on through travelers both make the puzzle worse, not better. Bypass volume and the weekday pattern do not connect traffic to restaurant revenue.
questions.why: The retail-shops and through-traveler options deepen the puzzle (fewer visitors, lower sales) instead of resolving it, which tempts students who match 'traffic' to 'revenue'.

questions.stem: In the argument, the statement that enrollment at public universities typically falls during recessions, whatever happens to tuition, plays which of the following roles?
options: It is an intermediate conclusion supported by the claim that the increases coincided with a recession.
It is evidence offered to show that higher tuition does not reduce enrollment.
It is a premise offered to show that the evidence cited by the analysts has an alternative explanation.
It is a claim made by the analysts that the argument goes on to reject.
It is a general principle from which the analysts derive their prediction.
questions.explain: The final sentence is the conclusion: the drop cannot by itself prove tuition caused it. The statement about recessions is a premise that supplies another possible cause of the drop. The intermediate-conclusion option is tempting because it is adjacent to the claim about the recession, but the statement is a premise that nothing in the argument supports. The argument does not claim tuition has no effect, and the statement is neither the analysts' own claim nor the source of their prediction.
questions.why: The argument only denies that the evidence proves the analysts' claim; it never asserts that tuition has no effect, and the recession statement is a premise, not a conclusion supported by the next sentence.

questions.stem: The official's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
options: assumes that every restaurant offering outdoor seating earned a top inspection score
relies on the results of inspections from only a single year
takes for granted that restaurants with outdoor seating are inspected more often than others
confuses the cleanliness measured by inspections with the quality of the food served
fails to consider relevant information about the restaurants that did not earn top scores
questions.explain: Without knowing how many of the other 160 restaurants offer outdoor seating, the 34 of 40 may reflect nothing but how common the feature is: if 85 percent of all restaurants had it, top scorers would too. The official makes no claim that every outdoor-seating restaurant scored highly, and the argument does not depend on inspection frequency or the food's quality. The single year is a minor weakness, not the central flaw.
questions.why: The figure 34 of 40 sounds impressive but means nothing without the base rate: if most restaurants in the district have outdoor seating, top scorers would show it anyway.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
options: On the islands that held both animals, feral cats did more harm to seabirds than rats did.
Eradicating rats does not by itself guarantee that seabird numbers will recover.
Seabird numbers on the cat islands would likely have recovered had the cats been removed along with the rats.
Where feral cats were present, the seabird decline was caused by the cats rather than by the rats.
Feral cats were present on most of the islands where rats were introduced.
questions.explain: On the islands that also held cats, removing the rats brought no recovery, so removing rats does not by itself guarantee recovery. The passage never compares the harm done by cats and rats, and never says what removing the cats would have done, though that is tempting. It does not say who caused the decline on the cat islands, and it gives no count of how many rat islands had cats.
questions.why: Each wrong option goes one step beyond the passage: the cats' relative harm, what removing cats would have done, who caused the decline on the cat islands, or how common cats were.
